subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF GOVERNMENT RESTRAINT PROGRAM TO UNIVERSITY TUITION FEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the six and five program was supposed to be a two-edged sword. Wages would be restricted to an increase of 6 per cent, but so would the price of goods and services; especially, the services provided by the Government directly or through agencies or funded programs.
Let us consider how university students, 500,000 strong across Canada, fared with the six and five program. Postsecondary education was one of the first victims of Government spending cutbacks. Over $100 million was sliced from the federal transfer payment in 1983. The shortfall must be recovered from private contributions and tuition fees.
This is what happened. In July, 1982, the then Secretary of State said that any increase in tuition fees would be held to the 6 per cent cap because of governmental funding. He was wrong. In Nova Scotia, university tuition fees increased on a range from 12 per cent to 16 per cent. Now Canadian university students face a second round of tuition fee increases for the 1983-84 academic year. Instead of the promised 5 per cent, some universities have already scheduled increases of 17 per cent and more; and additional expense of $150 or more for each student.
This financial burden is imposed in the face of alarming statistics related to student and youth unemployment. The Government is not only breaking its six and five promise, but it will also be throwing away the key to the future of many young Canadians.

June 27, 1983

The Government is committed to enhancing the role of women in all facets of our society. It is an ongoing and ever present commitment, clearly and unequivocally perceived. In order to ensure that this ongoing process is maintained and, indeed, strengthened, I propose the following. In view of the fact that 90 per cent of all legislation introduced into this House has a direct impact on women, and in view of the fact that all Cabinet documents now include a provision requiring status of women consideration, I propose a recommendation of the House to the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures. This recommendation would constitute the requirement that all terms of reference under which parliamentary standing committees, special committees and subcommittees operate, address and provide for status of women considerations.
It is my view, and one with which all of us in the House cannot help but concur, that this additional focus on the legislative impact on Canadian women will go a long way toward meeting the Government's commitment to true gender equality in all facets of Canadian life.

maintopic: NEW EMPLOYMENT EXPANSION AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
subtopic: EFFECT ON INDIAN COMMUNITIES AND INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not an exaggeration to say that today unemployment is the greatest threat to peace and stability in our society. It harms not only individuals but their families and communities as well. In an attempt to confront the problem, the federal government created the NEED Program. But this program has had little effect on Indian communities where unemployment soars as high as 90 per cent. It is in communities such as these where the NEED Program is most urgently required, yet it is precisely these communities that benefit least from it.
For example, wages for employees paid through the Department of Employment and Immigration are not to exceed $800 per month worked. Status Indians cannot, however, receive over $500 of NEED monies per month worked. This amounts to $300 less per month than the sum allotted to non-Indians. If this is not discrimination, I don't know what is!
Moreover, projects approved on Indian reserves are required to follow accounting, administrative, and monthly reporting procedures established for the initiative. This monthly accounting requirement, established by the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs, is substantially more onerous than that for projects approved through the Department of Employment and Immigration.
Thus, in Indian communities where unemployment is a potentially more hazardous problem than in non-Indian communities, less money has been made available to individuals, and greater obstacles to the initiation and management of work projects have been created.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CLEAN WATER TARGET PROPOSED FOR YEAR 2000 A.D.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the end of the second millennium is fast approaching. The year 2000 A.D. represents
2,000	years of the Christian era and will be a monumental landmark in the recorded history of mankind.
As a citizen of Canada and of the international community, I am concerned that our country should give considerable thought to how we might best utilize the year 2000 to try to resolve the recognized problems which continue to confront mankind, and to determine what solutions would best ensure that, barring natural occurences beyond man's control, the human race will continue to survive and evolve. With this end in mind, I feel that the Government of Canada should encourage the other nations of the world to work together to set goals both, at the national and international levels, focusing on improving the human condition by the year 2000. Such goals should include the establishement of suitable projects to be completed by the year 2000, both nationally and through cooperative efforts of countries around the world. One need only to reflect on such historic events as the eradication of smallpox to appreciate the symbolism.
A recommended project would be disinfecting contaminated drinking water which now exposes 600 million people to waterborne disease in depressed areas of the world. In the Third World, construction of drinking water and sewage systems would be expected to halve the incidents of disease such as typhoid, dysentery, cholera, and schistomiasis. Large-scale global efforts of this type could help to restore confidence in the international community and mankind over-all.

subtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over the past few weeks we have heard reports from a number of economic policy and forecasting institutions predicting massive levels of youth unemployment over the next several years. Most recently, Thomas Maxwell, head of the Conference Board of Canada, predicted that Canadian youth will face an unemployment rate of over 20 per cent in the next decade.
In May of this year there were 633,000 men and women between 15 and 24 years of age out of work. This represents 21.4 per cent of the workforce, an increase of 14,000 over the previous month. One of every five students who planned to return to school cannot find a job to help pay for it. Graduating students are forced to accept seasonal or part-time work, if they can find a job at all. The federal Government's feeble response is a youth job-creation program that will create fewer jobs than last year.
In the last fiscal year, federal, provincial and municipal Governments spent a total of $12 billion on education in Canada. We have encouraged youth to invest in education and career training-yet the Government and leadership of this country refuse to follow through with the long range economic planning necessary to make jobs a reality and not just a dream.
June 27, 1983

Youth and students want to work and want to contribute. They only need a reasonable opportunity to do so. The present Government offers them only fewer jobs and an economic situation which pushes them more and more into the stigma of welfare. The high rate of youth unemployment represents the unnecessary squandering of a precious national resource.

maintopic: SUPPORT URGED FOR DONATION OF BODILY ORGANS
SUPPORT URGED FOR DONATION OF BODILY ORGANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, many Canadians are alive today because of tissue and organ donation programs. There is, however, a serious shortage of organs needed for transplant operations. As the public becomes more aware of the possibilities for cure, and with spectacular medical breakthroughs happening more frequently today than ever before, it seems inevitable the demand for organs will increase.
In Ontario alone an average of 200 kidneys are donated and subsequently transplanted each year. As of May 25 there were more than 200 people waiting for kidney transplants. An average of 500 corneal transplants are performed each year in Ontario. By the end of April, 200 such transplant operations had already been undertaken and 78 people were still waiting.
Oral Questions
At the end of May, 90 children were being treated for pituitary dwarfism at the Hospital for Sick Children.
There is a proven need for organ donors in this country. Presently, people may voluntarily sign donor cards. In all but one of the ten Provinces, that is PEI, the consent form is on the back of a driver's licence. Ontario, however, is the only Province having a government sponsored central information agency.
A recent Gallup Poll indicated only 21 per cent of Canadians have signed organ donation cards. It is very important that the remaining 79 per cent of Canadians understand the serious shortage of organs for transplant and the opportunity they have, at no cost to themselves, to give a magnificent gift of a whole life to the many who wait for their help. We here as Members of Parliament, and all the men and women across Canada, can give this gift by signing the backs of our drivers' licences, or by signing a donor card available through our family doctors.

subtopic: PROCLAMATION OF YOUNG OFFENDERS LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Parliament has passed that Bill and I think there is a responsibility to proclaim it as soon as possible. The Hon. Member must bear in mind that that new regime will not work without the co-operation and support of the Provinces. In fact there are a number of additional programs that have to be introduced by the Provinces that are within their responsibility, before this legislation can be proclaimed. I do not think the Provinces should have the final say; I think Parliament should. But on the other hand, if the Provinces are proceeding in the spirit of the intention to implement the legislation, as I believe most are, then I think it is my responsibility and the responsibility of the Government to be very sympathetic to the problems that are experienced in implementing that legislation.
Dealing with the cost of implementing the legislation, there is no doubt that, under the Constitution, in the same way that it is a federal responsibility to finance federal correctional institutions, it is a provincial responsibility to finance these provincial institutions. Tremendous financial assistance has been provided in the young offender area over the years. 1 have indicated that we intend to maintain that assistance and increase it, but I cannot predict when satisfactory agreements will be reached with all of the Provinces. However, I can say that as long as the Provinces are moving forward in good faith to implement this major reform of the Government and of the Parliament, I cannot see myself forcing their hands on proclamation.

speechtext:
that Bill C-165, an Act to provide for financial assistance for industrial development in all regions of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Industrial and Regional Development Act
He said: Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure today to discuss Bill C-165, which provides a program for financial assistance to business and industry in all parts of Canada.
I apologize to my colleagues and to the Hansard reporters for my voice, Madam Speaker; I hope it does not fade too much before the end of my 20 minutes.
Let me begin by saying that the purpose of the Bill is very simple: it is to create and maintain long-term employment for Canadians from coast to coast. The program which will be authorized under the Bill is the Industrial and Regional Development Program which is being presented after much study by the private sector, by officials, my Cabinet colleagues and by Members of Parliament on both sides of the House.
Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced in early 1982 the reorganization of economic departments of Government which will result in the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, we have examined the need to ensure regional industrial development and the existing array of industrial support programs that have been available in DREE and ITC. The reasons were the same as those which spurred the decision to reorganize. There is a need, on the one hand, to rededicate ourselves to combating regional disparity in Canada and, on the other hand, we must ensure that industrial restructuring programs are actually geared to meet the circumstances which face Canadian industries in today's very competitive world market.
Regional disparity still exists in Canada despite the successful efforts of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which was launched some 14 years ago. These disparities not only place hardships on individual Canadians, but they also place a strain on the national fabric and detract from our ability to move forward as a unified nation in the pursuit of our common goals.
Combating regional disparity is difficult even in good economic times. With the onset of the recent world-wide recession, times have not been good. If it is difficult to offset regional disparities in times when our traditional industries in the industrial heartland are enjoying a period of strength, it is much more difficult in the period when, because of world-wide downturn, those traditional industries are suffering from soft markets, stiff international competition, rapid technological change and rising protectionism from the countries which make up our market. These circumstances demand a concerted action on the part of all Canadians, Governments at all levels and the private sector, both management and labour. With the reorganization of federal economic departments and the introduction of programs such as that contained in this Bill, the Government is trying to play its part in this concerted action.
The program outlined in this Bill has a number of features which are clearly recommended to the business community, to the Canadian public and to Hon. Members of Parliament. First and foremost, let us recognize that this program provides

June 27, 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
for the first time a regionally sensitized, multifaceted program of industrial financial assistance in all parts of Canada. I believe that is a point which has not been adequately emphasized in discussion of the program to date. This is not a program available only in certain designated regions; whatever riding any Hon. Member of this House represents, his or her constituents will be eligible for assistance under this program.
Another feature of this program is its flexibility. It is specifically designed to provide the type of assistance which is appropriate to a given industry, area or community at a given time. Hon. Members of this House well know that these needs vary greatly by region, by sector and over time in Canada. We have areas where the need is for greater investment and infrastructure in order to permit industries to establish and grow. We have areas where the need is for industrial diversification, the establishment of new plants or the launching of new product lines. We have areas and industries where the need is for innovation, to improve competitiveness.
These are more than needs. They are also tremendous opportunities, Mr. Speaker. They are opportunities to expand into the revolutionary growth industries of the future and opportunities to apply the benefits of technology and other innovations to virtually all of our existing industries in all parts of Canada, thus to ensure long-term viability and growth. We have great opportunities, through aggressive marketing techniques, to expand the international and domestic market for Canadian goods and services. This program addresses these needs and opportunities.
The program, Mr. Speaker, has yet another significant feature. In addition to the provisions I have listed, it adds a powerful new weapon to the federal Government arsenal in the continuing fight against regional disparity. The program recognizes not only the varied needs and opportunities of Canada's many regions, but also the levels of financial assistance required for effective industrial development across those regions. This program renews and renders more effective the commitment to regional economic development which underlay the establishment of DREE in 1969. It provides for the first time the levels of financial assistance specifically tailored to the level of disparity of the area concerned. Here we are not talking about broad geographic areas; we are talking about areas as small and specific as can be defined, using consistent, meaningful data which is available on a national basis. The method of using the data will be equitable, objective and subject to automatic regular review. It will provide the country's first consistent measure of regional disparity in Canada.
The mechanism I am referring to is the development index which uses data on employment, personal income and provincial fiscal capacity in order to provide a clear measure of the relative need for assistance. It will be applied to areas as small and specific as a single census district. Using the development index, areas of Canada are arranged at four levels or tiers of regional need. The first tier in which the basic level of support under the program will be provided contains the most developed 50 per cent of the population of Canada where there is a substantial need for industrial restructuring. In this tier, for example, financial assistance of up to 50 per cent of costs for
innovation of marketing activities will be provided and up to 25 per cent of modernization and expansion costs. There are three other tiers with increasing levels of support. For instance, in Tier IV areas, which contain the 5 per cent of the population living in areas of greatest need, the maximum level of support of the program is provided. Here, for example, up to 60 per cent of cost for plant establishment may be provided.
Since I first proposed this program during the budget debate, there have been several refinements to it. One of these refinements refers to the tier system. In any Tier I area where the unemployment ratio exceeds the national average by 1 per cent for any consecutive six-month period, that area will be provided with the next higher, or Tier II, level of assistance for establishment for one year. This is to provide for those instances where, for example, a cyclical downturn affects an area in the short term in a way which would not show up immediately by applying the development index, but where a short-term, although very real economic hardship nonetheless dictates a need for increased assistance. That is another example of the flexibility which is designed into this program.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the program provided for in this Bill, the Industrial and Regional Development Program, has been very carefully designed, after much consultation with the private sector and much discussion with my colleagues, to meet the general and specific goals of regional and industrial development in all parts of Canada. It provides for support over the whole range of industrial development needs, industrial infrastructure, industrial innovation, plant establishment, modernization, expansion, marketing and industrial restructuring or renewal. It provides support for these activities when and where they are needed in Canada. It provides for effective regional development by instituting a strong incentive to Canadian firms to invest in those areas of Canada which are in the greatest need of that investment.
I wish to remind Hon. Members that we have devised an organizational structure in the new department which will put the regional sensitivity and flexibility of this program into practice at the local level. We have been moving to put into place an organization based on decentralized expertise, decision making and local program delivery. We have combined the industrial sector expertise from ITC with the regional capacity of DREE. We have established regional offices in all Provinces, several new sub-offices, and more will open in the future.
We are working to establish a "one-stop shopping" approach to the Government assistance for business in our local offices. The local decision and delivery capacity of these offices should speed up the processing of applications significantly. The chief role of these offices is to make the Government services more widely available to businesses, particularly small and medium-size entrepreneurs. No longer will the business community have to travel to Ottawa to have access to federal information and assistance. The role of the people staffing these offices will be to get to know the business community and act as its advocate with the federal Government. They will take an
June 27, 1983

active role in informing firms of available Government support, all of which, incidentally, will be available locally for the first time.
1 have said, Mr. Speaker, that the new Industrial and Regional Development Program was devised with the benefit of consultation with the private sector. Let me assure the House that its implementation will be carried out in the same way. When referring to the private sector, I would like to reiterate that I mean business management and labour. I firmly believe, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stated in his budget, that in order to achieve our goals we must have the active participation of all the players in the game. For these reasons we will administer the new program, and indeed all programs of the Department, with the benefit of advice from the Industrial and Regional Development Board which will be co-chaired by representatives of management and labour, with membership from each group. The board will also have appropriate regional representation in its membership. By advising the Government, through our Department, on broad policy issues, the board will have an effective instrument to ensure the Government's industrial policy and programs are based on a broad consensus.
Another means to assist this effort, as Hon. Members will be aware, has been a move through our Department to establish sector-specific task forces or advisory committees, once again co-chaired by both management and labour. The efforts of these task forces will be of great benefit in terms of establishing our goals and strategies as far as the key industrial sectors are concerned.
Before concluding, I want to make clear the status of the general development agreements which have been administered by DREE. When the new structure for economic development departments was announced, there was some speculation as to the future of the general development agreements, or the GDAs, as Hon. Members call them, that were negotiated between DREE and the Provinces. I want to make it clear that those agreements are still in place and that subsidiary agreements will continue to be struck with the Provinces. GDAs will continue until their expiry in 1984 and negotiations for new agreements to replace them will take place in due course.
The administration of GDA activities has changed, however. Instead of a single Department, DREE, being responsible for administrative activities under the GDAs, this activity is now implemented by the various appropriate federal departments, including our Department, under the over-all co-ordination of the Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development.
1 firmly believe that what I have described today amounts to a major step forward in the rationalization, simplification and perfection of the federal Government's approach to both regional and industrial development objectives. I believe Hon. Members on both sides of the House have good reasons for
Industrial and Regional Development Act
supporting this exciting new Bill. At a time when some 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed, a concerted effort is needed for strengthening our industries. That need will increase as we strive for economic recovery in a world of rapid technological change and extreme competition. I believe it is timely, as the economic recovery takes hold, that we are proposing an improved method to ensure that our industrial strength increases in all parts of Canada.
Canadians who are watching the deliberations of the House I am sure will support me when I ask that we proceed with the Bill and get on with the job which must remain our first priority, that of creating meaningful and rewarding employment in all regions of Canada.
I would ask unanimous consent of the House, Mr. Speaker, to refer the Bill to the Standing Committee on Regional Development, rather than what was originally proposed by my colleague the House Leader, that it be sent to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

In some parts of the country only the DREE program was available and in other parts of the country only the IT&C programs were available. This program is one of those seven major programs and it will constitute approximately one-half of the total budget of the Department. In essence, with respect to areas comprising almost 50 per cent of the population of the country, industries located in those areas are not now eligible for financial assistance under the old RDIA program. In essence, we will not take the 50 per cent which is the most developed part of Canada and ensure
that it will have financial assistance for any company that wants to undertake modernization, expansion, innovation, design research and development, marketing or industrial renewal. Then we will take the 50 per cent of the country which is least developed and break it into three specific tiers, Tier IV being the bottom 5 per cent in terms of economic development in Canada. In turn, it will have the most enriched part of the program. We will then take the product cycle and the life cycle of a company and enrich the financial assistance, depending on in which of those four tiers a company is located. There is only one difference between the tiers outside of the degree of enrichment. For example, maximum assistance for modernization or expansion starts at 25 per cent of eligible capital costs for Tier I, 35 per cent for Tier II, 50 per cent for Tier III and 50 per cent for Tier IV.
The one element that is not available to the most developed part of the country is the new establishment. That has traditionally belonged to what we call the DREE-designated areas. In other words, if we allowed new companies in the most developed part of Canada to receive financial assistance, there would obviously be no reason, no justification whatsoever, for these companies to locate in the so-called disadvantaged areas of the country. That is the only element not included in each tier. It is important for Hon. Previously, if a riding was not designated, that means a Member's companies could not receive any financial assistance. From now on, they will receive financial assistance, but the enrichment will depend on the degree of economic disparity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to thank you for extending the question period. The questions were very useful and the Minister's answers will assist us a great deal in our deliberations.
Industrial and Regional Development Act
The Canadian family of Provinces and Territories has some poor and rich cousins. Since we captured our national dream and pushed the railroad through the mountains to the Pacific and developed our central manufacturing base with protective tariffs, we have witnessed the decline of the Atlantic region and the emergence of disparities which have grown and are with us today.
Distance from markets, high transportation costs, lack of capital, lack of entrepreneurship and associated skills are reflected in high unemployment, lack of industrial growth and a marked dependence on the transfer of federal funds. Wages and earned incomes remain well below the Canadian average. Other areas of Canada, notably the Gaspe region of Quebec, northern Ontario and specific regions in northern and western Canada can point to the same problems.
In the 1960s the federal Government addressed this problem with the ARDA program and the fund for rural economic development. Next came the Atlantic Development Board. In 1963 the Area Development Agency began providing assistance to the manufacturing sector. This assistance was quite properly directed to areas of high unemployment, but unfortunately it excluded major population and industrial centres in the Maritimes where new industries had the best chance of succeeding.
In 1968 we witnesed the formation of the first government department to deal exclusively with the problem of regional disparities. The special areas program and the Regional Development Incentives Act were powerful instruments in attacking the problem and together composed a clear indication of a strong dedication to regional development policy.
The initial thrust of DREE was to provide economic development in the lagging region east of Trois-Rivieres and certain areas where special needs existed. In time the areas designated for assistance were broadened and the impact of the DREE effort was diluted both by the enlargement of the scope of its operation and in the reduction of real dollars made available for that purpose.
In 1982 the reorganization for economic development split DREE in two and buried it in two departments of Government. DRIE now combines the program functions of DREE with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Given our national economic problems and the high unemployment facing Canada at the moment, it is understandable and desirable that the Government address these serious national issues, but surely the Government cannot be forgiven for not also addressing the problems of regional disparities. It should address both problems.
Any further diminution in the flow of funds to poorer regions can have very serious short-run consequences for individuals and provincial Governments and ultimately the national economy. In the long term it could be a catastrophe. The federal Government is now restricting the transfer of

June 27, 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
funds to provincial Governments with established funding programs and equalization by changes in the terms of the programs and by limiting increases.
I have no quarrel with better control over federal funds, but I do quarrel with the failure of the federal Government to recognize the impact that the reduction in transfer payments has on governments in the Atlantic Provinces which are nearly 50 per cent dependent on federal funds to maintain existing programs and standards of living.
The ultimate goal of federal development policies should be to create in the poorer Provinces a secondary manufacturing capability employing more wage earners and creating more taxpayers, so that ultimately the poorer Provinces can pull themselves up by their own bootstraps and have less dependency on transfer payments and equalization grants. At the moment, their limited ability to raise revenues through taxation or borrowing makes further reductions in the level of services an alternative which they are seeking desperately to avoid.
Also under assault by the madhatters in the Department of Transport is the historic and traditional assistance given to producers, manufacturers and shippers in the Atlantic Provinces since 1927 in the form of maritime freight rate subsidies. Any further reduction in this assistance could be disastrous to the Atlantic Provinces. It could mean a loss of $64 million to the Atlantic Provinces which would have to be made up by growers, industrialists and manufacturers which depend on transportation facilities, both within the Maritimes and for westbound exports. It could mean lost markets, lost incomes and lost jobs. It could mean declining use of regional resources for materials and decimation of competitive positions in central Canada.
The Maritimes population base is too small to absorb all its production. Major manufacturing plants have to sell outside the region, overseas, in the central committee market and, to a lesser degree, the western Canadian market. The long-haul shippers of Atlantic Canada have to put their goods in these markets at competitive prices or lose them. If the subsidies are removed, the Altantic manufacturing base, which we seek to develop, would be weakened and further centralization in Quebec and Ontario would follow. The rates have already been reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent with the prospect of complete elimination and utter catastrophe now facing Mari-timers.
The proposal contained in the Bill now before us will form the basis of DREE assistance in the future. It is a reformation of the Enterprises Development Program, the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program, the Regional Development Incentives Program and Support in Technology Enhanced Productivity Programs which have been restructured. Under this Bill, firms anywhere in Canada can qualify for assistance, which varies in degree according to a development index calculated for each of Canada's 260 census divisions. The index will be based on unemployment rates, the rate of employer per population ratio, income and the fiscal capacity of each Province.
The development index does not form a part of the Bill but is spelled out in the regulations, a copy of which has been given to us. The index contained in the regulations is different from the one mentioned by the Minister before committee a few weeks ago. Following our initial criticisms, and it is to his credit, it appears to have been improved, but since it is contained in regulations and not in the Bill, we do not know what it will be three weeks from now or even 30 weeks from now. Based on the value of the index, each census division will qualify for increases in levels of assistance according to its relative disparity on a four-tiered scale.
The new four-tier program represents a shift in direction from previous development initiatives and is a cause of some concern. I will express some potential programs. The Bill reshapes existing programs, many of which, like the Enterprises Development Program, were unsuited to the need of smaller companies in the Altantic Provinces and other areas suffering from disparity, and the mere restructuring of their application is unlikely to increase their impact.
Another major concern is that the impact of the development index is such that it does not operate at its maximum in the larger centres of industrial growth in the Atlantic Provinces and discriminates against them where average wages are higher and employment potential is better. It fails to recognize that it is in these larger centres that many people in outlying regions go seeking employment in industry and where they have a better likelihood of finding it. A failure to permit expansion to the maximum degree in these areas is a failure to provide the maximum number of potential jobs in industry that are badly needed. I am suggesting to the Minister that all of the Atlantic Provinces should be designated as qualifying for the highest tier of development assistance available.
The proposals contained in the legislation before us do not recognize the need for a concentrated approach to economic development beyond the boundary of a single census division. Consequently, many of the new programs can have limited application in the smaller census divisions in Atlantic Canada which have a limited industrial base and weak infrastructure.
Further, the incremental incentives appear inadequate to influence decisions on new plant locations and appear designed instead to concentrate on innovation and marketing, with the bulk of the funding going to the central manufacturing areas of the country. There is little stimulus to influence new plants to locate in the have-not regions that suffer greatest from disparities, and this is an essential element in any regional development policy.
In this latter regard, I would suggest to the Government that it consider the employment of a 150 per cent tax incentive, not as a grant but as a tax credit payable out of future tax by firms locating in areas that suffer from regional disparities, such as the Atlantic Provinces and the Gaspe region of Quebec. This incentive would be payable in respect to the capital cost of a new plant or an expanding plant and the cost of labour for the first three years of the plant's operation. This would not attract a single cent from our national Treasury because it would be
June 27, 1983

paid out of the income tax which such a firm would otherwise pay and is not now paying until the cost of the investment plus 50 per cent has been recovered. This proposal has worked effectively in other parts of the world, such as New Hampshire, and it is a proposal that has been brought forward by the prestigious New Brunswick Industrial Development Council.
I would also like to see the Government consider making the major ports in the Atlantic Provinces duty-free areas where low-cost products from the Third World can be imported and assembled in Canadian assembly plants according to Canadian specifications, using Canadian technology and Canadian workers and then be exported to markets of the world, the same as is done in Amsterdam, Singapore and 16 ports in the United States of America under its highly successful DISC Program.
Clearly there should be a renewed and continued strong commitment made by the federal Government to the development of the economy of Provinces that suffer from the effects of regional disparity so that those Provinces can become less dependent on transfers from the federal Government. They key to such a change is reduction in regional disparities by lowering unemployment rates and taxation levels and raising per capita incomes.
High transportation costs, a weak industrial base and limited infrastructure are fundamental issues that must be addressed. I suggest that economic development can best be achieved within a framework of co-operation between federal and provincial Governments and industry and labour. Consideration must be given to the winners in the Canadian economy and the promotion and growth of an industrial base must surely be founded on the strength of the resource base and access to markets. Infrastructure development has a strong supporting role.
The Government's development policies have been consistently eroded by its monetary policy, which has been insensitive to the unfair and unequal impact it has on disadvantaged regions such as Atlantic Canada. Atlantic Canada is the first hit, the hardest hit and the last to recover from the Government's tight money policies and the Bank of Canada's heedless and stubborn refusal to consider ameliorating measures.
The bottom line is that there is no longer a federal Government department with the sole mandate of promoting development in the least developed regions of the country. The demise of DREE and the broadening of areas for regional development suggest a change in the singular emphasis put on the reduction or elimination of regional disparities. This comes at a time when other federal programs, including equalization payments and transportation subsidies, are coming under review.
Details for implementation of the programs outlined in this Bill and the dollars that are to be made available for each region have not yet been made public. The notational estimates and comparisons between existing programs and new programs on a regional basis are important. We feel that it is essential that full disclosure of the nature of the new program and its
Industrial and Regional Development Act
dollar impact on each region be made in committee to permit a proper evaluation. Is the new program another cosmetic or can it be adapted to the needs of our regions and made to address our serious national and regional problems? I sincerely hope it can, and that is why we are making constructive suggestions and looking forward with great anticipation to a good dialogue on this very important measure in committee.
Canada urgently needs policies to stimulate innovation, improve productivity and enable Canadian enterprises to put Canadian goods in foreign markets at competitive prices. Canada needs policies to put Canadian goods in Canadian markets at competitive prices. Canada needs policies to address regional disparities. To a degree, this Bill seeks to address all three needs, and we must have a good discourse in committee in order to determine to the best of our ability as Parliamentarians whether it achieves each of those objectives. That is why I look forward to seeing the Bill go to committee as soon as possible, and I join the Minister in that regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not plan to ask the Hon. Member a question. I want to put a few statements on record.
I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, to be afforded this opportunity today to respond to Bill C-165, an Act to provide for financial assistance for industrial development in all regions of Canada. I want to say that we in the New Democratic party are more than anxious to get this Bill into committee as expeditiously as possible in order to carry out the fine tuning of Bill C-165 that we feel is necessary and get it back into the House for quick passage in order that it can be enacted early in the month of July.
1 must say, Mr. Speaker, that I find it interesting that the reason we are discussing this Bill today, a Bill that recognizes the reality of regional inequality in the country, goes back to the very beginning of Confederation when Sir John A. Macdonald, a Conservative Prime Minister, introduced something called the national policy. In this policy, the central part of Canada was identified as the area where Canada would do its manufacturing and Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario and northern Quebec, the Prairies, British Columbia and the Territories would be subservient to central Canada. These areas would be the hinterland to the industrial heartland made up of the lower St. Lawrence Valley.
We have now recognized, Mr. Speaker, that not only must these regional inequalities be overcome if we are to bring equity and justice to the Canadian economic landscape, but I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) and the Minister responsible for regional expansion has had to agree that the present policies are anything but equitable. I would simply refer to two or three of the existing policies that I think demonstrate most clearly the injustices that are inherent in existing Government programs when it comes to providing economic opportunities for all parts of Canada.
In the period April to November, 1982 one Province received $30 million in development incentives while British

June 27, 1983
Industrial and Regional Development Act
Columbia received only $558,000 during that same period. On a worker basis, Mr. Speaker, this averaged out to $10.48 for every worker in that unnamed Province and only 41 cents for every worker in British Columbia. Similar figures for 1981 show an even stronger trend in favour of this special Province. That Province received $25.77 per worker compared to only 56 cents per worker in British Columbia. While we recognize that there are differences between Provinces, I believe this demonstrates unquestionably that present Government programs, for a whole variety of reasons, favour certain constituencies and certain regions of Canada.
Another demonstration of that is the work presently being done by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. That corporation is in place to bring foreign requests for goods and supplies to Canadian suppliers of those goods and supplies. A few weeks ago in the Finance Committee, representatives of the Canadian Commercial Corporation were asked what percentage of the business done by the corporation was done in conjunction with suppliers from the Province of British Columbia. Many of us were not surprised when the answer turned out to be just less than 1 per cent. Just less than 1 per cent of all of the business done by the Canadian Commercial Corporation is done in conjunction with firms from the Province of British Columbia.
All sorts of examples of the really profound injustice attached to the various Government programs could be indentified. One could say that these programs are based, by and large, on patronage and on porkbarrelling techniques.
I think that some of the best listening to be done these days, Mr. Speaker, is to be done by Members of Parliament when listening to members of such Departments as Industry, Trade and Commerce and DREE who have resigned from positions that they have perhaps held for a number of years and are now involved in some other pursuits and they sit down to reflect off the record to Members of Parliament what really has gone on in those Departments. I believe that what one finds, Mr. Speaker, is a considerable amount of what can only be described as patronage.
I am pleased to say that the present Minister, by introducing Bill C-165, has taken a major step to eliminate that kind of behaviour and in fact to make an effort to deliver an equitable industrial incentive program for all parts of Canada. We were disappointed with much of the behaviour of DREE over the past few years. While we recognize that many positive initiatives were taken by DREE, we also recognize that vast areas of the country were not designated. Areas of western Canada where for years and years the unemployment rate was 20 per cent or 25 per cent still have not been designated. The latest fiasco with the ILAP designation is almost laughable. Some areas whose problems did not begin to approach the greater problems of other areas were designated because of the political bias that exists in the system. The work done on Bill C-165, however, does much to dispel the sour taste associated with so many Government programs designed to provide industrial incentives.
The New Democratic Party feels that by identifying the various tiers the Bill will identify the criteria required to bring a number of industrial location factors into play. I should like to identify four or five problem areas that should be clarified in committee. There are problems for the small business sector with this Bill. I think every Member of the House recognizes the fact that the small business sector of the economy has been hardest hit in recent times. The "mom and pop" operations in the country are struggling to survive. They hope for a positive response from the Government as they see their large cousins receiving all kinds of financial handouts or making favourable arrangements with financial institutions. They themselves, however, are fighting the battle in the trenches without very much ammunition.
We must ask whether Bill C-165 provides encouragement for the small business sector. I realize the Bill must have limits but this sector of the business community must receive very serious consideration in the provision of industrial development grants.
The fact that the development index is found only in the regulations attached to the Bill means that the index can be changed by the Department without difficulty. Members of the committee will want to make sure that the present index has been arrived at carefully and that the formula used to trigger the provision of incentives for a particular region will perform equitably across the country.
In committee the Minister will have to let us know exactly how much money is attached to the program. I am sure the Minister and his Department will be sensitive to the rgional distribution of funds in view of their commitment to decentralization. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has pointed out that this might also be interpreted as centralizing and moving away from the close federal-provincial discussions of the past. Nevertheless, as the Government indicates its intention to decentralize decision making for industrial incentive grants, the regional distribution of funds across the country must reflect the economic needs in any particular year.
The Minister has said that emphasis will be placed on one-stop shopping for the small enterpreneur but we have to wonder just how that will take place. I certainly agree with Members who spoke earlier and said that the average business person having to journey to Ottawa to beg for funds for their business or for a particular region or municipality is something that we must stop. We hope that the Bill will accomplish this. We wonder, however, whether the availability of one-stop shopping is well known to the business community. The maze of red tape that surrounds Government programs discouraged many in the small business community from seeking help. The large firms have professionals on staff who make the approach for them but the small entrepreneur must be able to go directly to a source which is accessible if the program is to be equitably administered across Canada.
I hope that when the committee has an opportunity to examine the fine points of the Bill and the regulations in detail
June 27, 1983

the Minister will indicate how he plans to serve the very small entrepreneur. The Bill is designed to provide financial assistance for industrial development in all regions of Canada but it fails to address the serious problems faced by small entrepreneurs and native people. I realize that any Bill cannot be all things to all groups but 1 hope that in committee the Minister will address the ways and means by which the native communities can be assisted with industrial and economic development.
We are quite enthusiastic about the Bill, Mr. Speaker, because of what it can do for communities in the country. As an example I will use the community of Kamloops, British Columbia, but I could use any community. The legislation seems almost too good to be true at this point; it almost seems just to have come from the Liberal benches. Let me take the example of a firm in the Tier II ranking which is interested in locating in the Kamloops region. It would be eligible for up to 50 per cent for innovation, more specifically research and development funding; 35 per cent funding for capital costs for a new or expanded veature; 35 per cent support for modernization of plant or expansion of plant; 60 per cent assistance for introducing new marketing techniques and approaches; and 25 per cent support for renewal.
I believe that is going to assist those development officers or development commissioners, whatever title they may have in different parts of Canada, when they go about approaching firms to relocate in their regions, whether it is Canadian firms wishing to open up a new branch, whether it is larger corporations which might be interested in opening up facilities in Canada, or perhaps investors wanting to open up a new venture, particularly in one of the non-growth areas of our country. I believe it will assist them considerably when they are able to go to an investor and say: "This is what we are able to offer you at this point; based on the existing economic situation in our community, these are the incentives we have in place which are provided by the federal Government". I believe this is going to have the potential of making quite a substantial improvement, Mr. Speaker.
In closing, 1 would simply say that as we move to a program which I believe will be a more equitable program in terms of providing industrial and economic opportunities to the regions of Canada, other than Central Canada, which obviously has a number of built-in advantages already, we must be careful when we are simply forcing growth into areas where it may normally not go. There is an underlying assumption that by providing incentives and grants we can make an enterprise economically viable almost by definition. We all know that this is not true, Mr. Speaker. The list is long of all kinds of economic endeavours in this country which are laughable when it comes to economic viability. Even at the moment of their inception, people knew these incentives were not being provided because of an economic need which was real. They were not economically viable but were politically viable. It made political sense.
Industrial and Regional Development Act

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, April 19, 1983, consideration of Bill C-95, an Act to provide for Government operated pool systems on combinations of athletic contests and events and to amend the Criminal Code and the Income Tax Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture; and Motion No. 2 (Mr. Reid, St. Catharines).

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in my place in opposition to Bill C-95, a Bill to establish a sports pool, particularly to speak to the first amendment, Motion No. 2, which calls for the striking of Clause 14(b) which states:
To conduct and manage, in accordance with regulations made by the Governor in Council, such lawful gaming activities as the Governor in Council directs.
We have all seen how Crown corporations of the Government have conducted and managed our affairs vis-a-vis the post office, Canadair, de Havilland, et cetera, and we have also seen the regulations made by the Governor in Council which, in essence, come down from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). However, before going into this part of it in depth, I would like to say that as a Member of Parliament one of our many rights, one which I prize, is our availability to what is known as the householder. This small booklet, composed by
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
Members and distributed to each household, can be mailed out four times a year, as Your Honour is aware.
In each of my householders, I include a questionnaire covering a wide range of topics. I do this intentionally because as a Member of Parliament I am only an extension of my constituents and their views. It is important to me that 1 reflect as accurately as possible these views. I receive a substantial number of responses to each questionnaire, into the many hundreds. The results of these polls greatly assist me in determining the feelings of my constituents on issues of the day.
In July of last year, one of the questions posed in my householder was as follows: "Do you favour a sports betting pool administered by the federal Government?" Seventy-five per cent of those responding answered no, 70 per cent said yes, and 8 per cent were undecided. Obviously, the majority of the people in my riding are against the creation of a sports pool. I stand here today, as is my duty, to register their opinion in this House.
The striking of the clauses is what we are discussing, and Clause 14(b) would allow the sports pool corporation to conduct and manage such lawful gaming activities as the Government directed. A federal re-entry, if you will, into the lottery field would thus be possible for any game imaginable. It is just too broad. Again, it involves the element as to whether we trust the people across the way to come back into the lottery field. Video slot machines paying cash for a win instead of a free replay is one game, and the Government might now be considering something such as that. We find the clause is just absolutely too offensive to the Provinces, with which we have an agreement on lotteries, and too open-ended in the directions that it can take to let it go unchallenged. That is why I am on my feet.
As I just intimated, this new lottery or sports pool would involve a Crown corporation. It is only a few short weeks since the Auditor General, in his annual report to Parliament, expressed strong unease and a clear caution with regard to Crown corporations, something he rightly termed "subgovernments". We are all aware of what has been happening. All one must do is pick up this morning's newspaper to see the Auditor General again decrying what happened with Canadair.
Does the Government see the problem? Does the Government hear the warnings? I think not. Does the Government say anything in response? No, it just blames management. Yet in this very clause it wants to take over management and responsibility again in the sports pool. It wants to create another Crown corporation. That is its arrogant answer, as if we had not had enough Canadairs.
The sports pool corporation to be created by this Bill will conduct and manage a federal sports pool. Why should there be another Crown corporation? Why should there be a sports pool to begin with? The Government just loves Crown corporations. It has over 300 of them now, most of them unaudited and uncontrolled. Air Canada, VIA Rail, the Commercial Investment Corporation and others are available to the Government to use as a means of rewarding its people, taking care of its own. There is Petro-Canada, which 69 per cent of

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
Canadians do not go out of their way to use and which 45 per cent feel should be sold.
Is there another failed Liberal or miffed Liberal out there somewhere who needs some place to hang his hat and some money to line his pocket? Is that why the Government needs another Crown corporation?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I think so, as my hon. colleague says. The Government says the sports pool is needed to aid fitness and amateur sport and arts and culture. Which cultured Liberal out there in the boonies is waiting for the call to show what a sport and how fit he is to run this newest enterprise? I a wait this appointment with bated breath. It will help fund the 1988 Calgary Olympics, we are told, and we are very pleased about that. We know that concerning anything that happens in Alberta, the money will be well spent. No one is denying that this event is worthy of our support, and we totally do support it. However, there must be a better, more sensible way of doing this, not a Jean Drapeau philosophy involved.
Back in the late 1960s, those same Montreal Olympics incurred a deficit of about $1 billion, and all three levels of Government, Montreal, Quebec and the federal Government, began looking for ways to pay the deficit. The Quebec Government suggested that the federal Government take over the Olympic lottery which was due to expire in 1976. As a result, Loto Canada was created. It, of course, was a Crown corporation. Loto Canada was given a three-year mandate, and its establishment was supported by all major political Parties, with the exception of the socialists to my left. The lottery made quite a great deal of money and the Government of the day, like the one now, warmed to the idea of carrying on this profitable undertaking. It meant more taxpayers' dollars to squander.
Early in 1979, a Bill was introduced in the House to make Loto Canada a permanent lottery corporation. Opposition support for this move was negative. Loto Canada had been scandal-ridden over the course of its existence. The Provinces argued that lotteries were a provincial area of concern and threatened court action. We in Opposition reminded the Government that it had promised in 1976 not to extend the lottery unless the Provinces consented. The issue was finally put to the voters of Canada. The Liberal platform called for the continuation of the lottery under redefined terms. We called for the dismantling of Loto Canada in return for an agreement with the Provinces on lottery revenues. In my view as a federalist, it was a very wise decision. We won the election and soon after gave the Provinces exclusive jurisdiction over lotteries in return for $24 million annually, indexed to 1979. This money was to be split fifty-fifty between arts and culture, fitness and amateur sport, a far cry from what the Bill before us is providing.
The Provinces also agreed to assume responsibility for the federal share of the costs related to the expansion, upgrading and renovation of three National Hockey Leagues arenas. Shortly after the agreement was signed, Parliament dissolved for the 1980 election. During the election campaign, the Liberals promised they would do everything possible to get the
federal Government back in the lottery business. However, once in office they were informed by their legal advisers that the Conservative Government's agreement was binding enough to make any breach of that agreement a serious matter.
I would now like to turn to the crux of the whole issue. The loophole-lookers took over and the loophole they latched on to was that of a sports pool. With a lottery ticket, winning is simply a matter of luck. A sports pool ticket meant involving some skill. That was the loophole for the federal Government to break its word to the Provinces and get back into the lottery business. The reason was the Government's distinction between "luck" and "skill". Based on this reasoning, the Government announced in the fall of 1981 that it would seek the establishment of the Sports Pool Corporation.
I see that my time is running out. I had a lot more that I wished to say on the subject but suffice it to say that we on this side of the House and Canadians do not trust the Government to run a sports pool. We do not know what it will do with the money. The definition is too broad. We think that Clause 14(6) should be deleted completely. We believe that regional and provincial disparity exists and that the federal Government has no business adding to the problem. I strongly urge all Members to consider this Bill very carefully and not aid and abet the Government in its sweeping powers under a sports lottery.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say a few words about Bill C-95. My colleague has pointed out some of the pitfalls to be anticipated in an inept Government trying to handle a potentially scandal-ridden business.
I would confine my remarks to the potential effect that this Bill will have on one of Canada's valuable and loved industries, the horse racing business. It could be seriously damaged by the loss of some $300 million which will be taken from the disposable income of Canadian earners.
This penchant for raising money, a form of hidden taxes, by a Government which has a penchant for raising money from any source whatever totally disregards the damage which will be done to this important taxpaying business. Surely some consideration should be given to this valuable industry other than just excluding it from pool betting.
Who will protect or replace the lost jobs, the lost revenues and the lost enjoyment of Canadians if standardbred or thoroughbred horse racing is damaged beyond recovery? The Government-inspired recession is already taking its toll of the nation's racetracks. Attendance is down over 2 per cent this year and betting is down over 3 per cent. That is the official statement. In fact, in the last quarter the reality is that attendance and betting are down approximately 15 per cent.
Horse racing goes back some 3,500 years. It is an old and honoured entertainment medium. It is a sport. An afternoon in the sun watching horses run or taking one's spouse out for dinner at the track is far superior to keeping a clammy lottery
June 27, 1983

ticket in one's pocket in the hope of becoming an instant millionaire against totally ridiculous odds. The track does not have the climate of a Nevada casino. It is a place where people go to have a thoroughly good time, not lose much money and perhaps even make a little. But it is always to enjoy the sport.
The horse racing business employs 50,000 people or more in Canada. These people depend on the profitability of the industry, as in any other business, for their livelihood. In effect, racetracks are the employer of horsemen, trainers, farriers, veterinarians, farmers who grow the feed and so on. It is even the employer of people who serve in the restaurants and gasoline operators who sell gasoline to the people who come to the racetrack. The spin-offs are wide and unlimited.
There are approximately 15,000 registered race horses in Canada today. One can see that there are three jobs for Canadians for every horse that is raced. There are 3,000 throughbred and standardbred breeders in Canada who employ grooms, trainers and others, all of whom pay taxes. There are 10,000 race horse-owners in Canada. All of these
50,000	people are already in some jeopardy as tracks cut back on the size of their purses and costs because of the general recession.
The largest single sporting event, certainly in North America if not in the world, is the Kentucky Derby in Louisville, Kentucky, a city of 300,000 people. Just yesterday, thousands of Canadians enjoyed the Queen's Plate at Woodbine in Toronto, and others the Confederation Cup at Flamboro in the standardbred racing business.
Simply consider some of the people involved in horse racing and some of the skills involved, not to mention the investment dollars, to raise Canadian horse breeding to world standards in order to appreciate that this is indeed a full-fledged industry. They include the trainers, the drivers, the jockeys, the owners who are people with the finances and the love of horse racing. They are people like E. P. Taylor. Look what he has done with Windfield Farms and the breeding industry and racing in Ontario. He has a great success record. As well, there is Louie Levesque, the Speers family on the Prairies and dozens of smaller operators who are dedicated to the achievement of excellence in the breeding business in Canada.
What is the point here? The point is that the $300 million which will be removed from the disposable income of Canadians will adversely affect the racing business. Let me cite a quotation:
1 want to say that there is every indication that the operations of these sports pools will not harm horse racing in any way.
That was said by the Hon. Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) to the Communications and Culture Committee hearings on Bill C-95 last December, 1982. 1 can tell the Hon. Minister that the $300 million taken from the pockets of Canadians will affect this industry at a time when the recession and proliferation of multi-channel satellite TV video games and other competing interests will severely affect the racing business and keep people away from the tracks.
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
The tracks need more money for special events, track improvements and public relations in general, not less money while Canadians buy lottery tickets which support nothing but an unproductive and increasing bureaucracy. At a time when this valuable tax-paying industry is scraping for every dollar, just as other businesses in Canada are today, this is no time to be leaching $300 million out of taxpayers' pockets in competition. What Canada does not need now is another lottery and another Government money grab. If culture, sports and medical research are deserving of increased funding, and 1 believe they are, they should be funded adequately by regular governmental support after due parliamentary debate and should not be subject to the vagaries of revenue pools based on the variable degree of public support in the buying of lottery tickets.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the Government is fed up with arresting bookies for taking bets on football games and is now making it all quite legal and respectable in the hope of turning a quick profit.
I want to make it clear for the record that Bill C-95, which seeks to establish a Government's sports pool, is blatant interference in the affairs of the Provinces of this nation. It is greatly exaggerated in terms of potential for profit and will have a negative effect, I believe, in many other areas as well. Lotteries have traditionally been the exclusive domain of the Provinces; that is, until Loto Canada was voted into existence in order to help finance the huge deficit incurred by the 1976 Olympics.
Loto Canada had the support of all major political parties mainly because it was considered only a temporary fundraising device and contained an agreement to share revenue with the Provinces; that is, one-eighth of the profits. However, the Liberals, following along in their tradition of "Give them an inch and they will take a mile", decided that if three-years of Loto Canada is a good thing, then indeed a permanent Loto Canada would indeed be wonderful. However, here in the Opposition corner we believe in the merit principle; that is, if a notion has merit we support it. But after three years of existence Loto Canada had lost its shine. It had been scandal-ridden over the course of its very short existence. The Provinces were threatening court action and wanted the complete pie, not just a slice of the action. As well, we knew full well that the Government had promised not to go ahead with extensions of the lottery corporation without the consent of the Provinces. Therefore, in our opinion, Loto Canada was no longer worthy of merit and we ceased to support it.
The sports pool was the offspring of the controversy over Loto Canada. The Government, squandering money so merrily, finally had to think of new and tricky ways to raise it. It was aware of the Provinces' continued opposition to any form of federal lottery. Not only that, but the federal Government was aware of the Opposition Parties' continued abhorrence of any proposal to create a clone of Loto Canada. Therefore, some bright light in a Government office came up with the idea of having a sports pool.

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
A sports pool could not be considered to be a bona fide lottery and therefore the federal Government would be immune to any attacks from the Provinces on the basis that revenues thus raised belonged to the latter. Not only that but the element of skill involved in selecting a winner in a baseball or table tennis match removed the potential objection that these things would attract foolish gamblers throwing away their life's earnings without a hope of winning.
The federal Government hoped this would take care of church groups and other dissenters who feel that gambling is not necessarily one of life's most desirable occupations. Not only was this form of gambling less risky and therefore more desirable for people on which to blow their pay cheques but the proceeds would go to fitness and amateur sport. You would not refuse to buy Girl Guide cookies, would you, Mr. Speaker? After all, the proceeds are going to a useful and well established group. Unfortunately, such a comparison does not ring true. The Government is trying to tell us that the proceeds from its new corporation are going to go to good causes. Why not be honest and tell us that, after all is said and done and the hefty salaries have been paid to all the fat cat executives who will be appointed as heads of this new sports pool corporation, probably only peanuts will be left for the amateur sport community?

When an athletic group or volunteer organization tries to go door to door to collect funds, people will say: "I'm sorry, I can't support you. You guys get your money from the Government, go ahead and apply to the Grits; apply to the Government." In effect, the money coming from the Government effectively deters normal fund raising. When the fine print is read, there is not even an assurance to the taxpayer that the funds generated by the sports pool will even go to the proper and most desirable places. Some of the proposed beneficiaries of the sports pool include fitness and amateur sport, arts and culture, medical research, the Calgary Olympics and worthy capital projects. What proportions are to go to each body is one question I would ask. What is the definition of a worthy capital project? Would it be something built in my riding as a Conservative Member? It would be wonderful if the House of Commons were made aware of the specifics of this deal, thus helping to avoid some of the scandal involved in the Loto Canada fiasco. There should be no wording in the proposed Bill which leaves potential for abuse. Not only that, but with so many beneficiaries, no one segemnt is likely to receive a significant benefit from the winnings. That is, of course, assuming that the sports pool is profitable at all. We have no guarantee of that.
The Minister responsible has high hopes for the success of the sports pool. He states optimistically that the net annual return will be in the order of $80 million. A more realistic assessment was provided by the Ontario Minister of Tourism and Recreation. He puts the gross annual return of such an endeavour to be in the area of $30 million to $40 million. This is based on the dismal weekly sales figures of the Quebec hockey pool. If you cannot sell hockey in Quebec, then you cannot sell lemonade in the desert or a sports pool to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join this debate. I want to get something on the record right now in terms of the position the Government is taking with respect to a sports pool. The Government is speaking with a forked tongue. The Government is a prevaricator. The Government is telling the people of Canada a story exactly opposite to the truth. The Government is misleading the Canadian public with respect to the basis upon which it enters into the sports pool, and the Government is to be severely chastised by thinking Canadians for the position it has taken.
I want to explain this basic fundamental proposition that I put forward. It is a factual proposition which will be understood by the vast majority of Canadians. I will relate the history of this matter.
During the time when we were the Government of Canada, the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) and the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) entered into an arrangement to get the federal Government out of the lottery business. They entered into an arrangement with provincial Governments by which it was agreed that provincial Governments would accept the responsibility of carrying on their existing lotteries and the federal Government under contract would remove itself from the position of carrying on lotteries on the federal side. When the Government across the way came into power, it was in a dilemma as to how to circumvent the contractual arrangement that had been entered into by the then Government of Canada. Of course, moral implications were not of concern, nor were the legal considerations, and it finally came upon a device known as the sports pool to take itself slightly out of the ambit of a lottery in the strict legal sense of the term.
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
Now the Government has a system which was modelled upon Hockey-Select in the Province of Quebec. In order to justify this unfortunate departure from every sense of principle and legal commitment, it had to find a justification to say to Canadians, "Support us in the creation of this new sports pool". Then it glommed on to the Calgary Winter Olympics by saying to Canadians, "Everyone in Canada needs to support the Calgary Olympics which will take place in 1988, but in order to finance it we need the new sports pool legislation to be passed", ob
When I talk about prevarication, forked-tongue and the federal Government saying something contrary to the truth of the matter, this is an example which can be documented. The commitment of the federal Government to support the Calgary Olympics was not tied to any sports pool. In fact, there was no specific undertaking that the sports pool or any form of lottery or other gambling device would be used to support the Olympics. The commitment was clear and unequivocal. Even the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), who got to where he is today on the basis of being one of the outstanding counsel in the small debts courts of Quebec, will agree that this proposition was really not worthy of any government representing the people of Canada.
Another example of how the federal Government speaks out of both sides of its mouth was evident in the application made to the Superior Court of the Province of Quebec in which judgment was handed down on January 26, 1983. The applicant was the Attorney General of Canada, representing the Government of Canada; the respondent was Loto-Quebec; and the Attorney General of Quebec was an intervenor. It was an application for an injunction by the federal Government against the Province of Quebec to prevent it from carrying on Hockey-Select. I would like to indicate what was said by the federal Government on that occasion. Quoting from the judgment of Mr. Justice Rene Hurtubise who rendered his decision on January 26, 1983, he said:
We will first examine the arguments of the Attorney General of Canada.
Specifying that he is acting as guardian of justice and in the interests of the public ... which satisfies us as to his interest in this proceeding, the Attorney General of Canada puts forward principally the following arguments:
-positively, the contest Hockey-Select constitutes a pool-selling game or "a system designed to promote bookmaking, pool selling or betting on a sporting event, the whole being prohibited by Section 186 of the Criminal Code";
-negatively, Hockey-Select is not a lottery;
-alternatively, even if it was a lottery, Hockey-Select is a pari-mutuel system from the beginning to the end of the contest and, therefore, falls within the exception to the exception, namely within the scope of paragraph (6) of Section 190 Cr.C.
Then he went on to say:
At paragraphs 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 18, he explains the underlying reasons for the motion:
He was referring to the Attorney General of Canada at that point. The federal Government stood in court to save the people of Quebec from this dastardly Hockey-Select which was poisoning the minds of the people of that Province; the Government of Canada was the saviour of the conscience of the
