people of that Province. First the Government said that it wanted:
-to prevent the continuation of the illegal operation of Hockey-Select;
-to stop the public inducement to act illegally;
-not to permit Hockey-Select to continue when the federal Parliament considers amending the Criminal Code in that respect;-
-to underline that it is against public order and morality for anyone, including a mandatary of Her Majesty in the rights of the Province of Quebec, to contravene the provisions of the Criminal Code.
If I have ever heard duplicity, if I have ever heard a federal government speaking out of both sides of its mouth, this is an example. It wanted to save the morals of the people of the Province of Quebec. At the same time it brought before Parliament legislation to create a sports pool, a lottery, a parimutuel, a gambling device on which it would, on the basis of what it said in court in that instance, undermine the morals of the people of Canada. The Government is inducing people to carry on gambling which is illegal for any other institution or for any other person in Canada. Yet the federal Government finds itself in the position now of doing the very thing of which it accused the Province of Quebec in terms of Hockey-Select.
On the basis of the representations I have heard, the people of Canada are now fast realizing the fact that this particular proposition for a gambling pool has no basis of relationship to the Calgary Olympics; it has no validity because of the Calgary Olympics. More and more Canadians are becoming concerned about the moral side of the federal Government involving itself in lotteries, pools or gambling devices which are a tax on people least able to afford it. Gambling is a tax on the poor. It is a tax on people who try with what little money they have to invest in a ticket in order to attain some sort of monetary independence. It is a sad, sad proposition when the federal Government is so unable to manage its affairs that it creates a tax on the poor people of Canada.
Today I received a telegram which I would like to read. It reads:
On May 29th over 500 delegates to Saskatchewan Conference, United Church of Canada, unanimously passed a resolution to urge the Government of Canada to abandon its intention to re-enter the lottery and gambling field in any way including sports pool. Please do all you can to stop Bill C-95.
It was signed by Merv Harrison, Chairman of the National Working Unit on Social Issues and Justice. The United Church of Canada understands what is going on here; the people of Canada understand. I oppose this legislation because it is wrongheaded and deceitful. It is based upon the premise that the poor people of Canada have to support the mismanagement of the Government. The Government of Canada ought to do better, carry out its contractual obligations, stay out of the lottery business and do Canadians a big favour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak to Bill C-95 at report stage, in particular to Motion No. 2 in the name of my good friend the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). Before getting into my presentation proper, I want to avail you of some fine remarks made in 1732 by Henry Fielding who said at that time:
A lottery is a taxation,
Upon all the fools in creation;
And Heav'n be prais'd,
It is easily rais'd.
Credulity's always in fashion:
For folly's a fund Will never lose ground.
While fools are so rife in the nation.
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
In the eyes of the Liberal Party, there are many fools in this nation who can be persuaded to give up some of their hard-gotten gains so that hon. gentlemen opposite can spend it as they see fit. My colleague to my left gave some illustrations of how they have spent some of this money already.
The argument over lotteries, both private and state-run, has waxed and waned for hundreds of years. In some research that I performed in the last five minutes, I found that it was in 1826 that the last British state-run lottery was held. At that time a Bill was passed which outlawed state-run lotteries. It heralded an era of Victorian morality. This concept of morality spread across what is now know as the Commonwealth, and also come to Canada at that time.
My personal preference is not to have state-run lotteries. It had been my intention to make the argument in favour of that position on the basis of morality and ethics, but I realized the futility of arguing on the basis of ethics and morality in a House that is dominated by Liberals. If we are to have this type of gambling activity in Canada, and it is not necessary for us to put it all aside, I would prefer that it remain within the private domain rather than be conducted by Governments, whether they be at the federal or provincial level. The main reason for this is that if we are to have gambling, it must be subject to certain strict controls. Whether that gambling be horse racing tracks, dog racing tracks, bingos or any other form of gambling, it is impossible for the Government on the one hand to be the regulator and policeman and make sure that these things are run properly and honestly and on the other hand to be a player in the game. It is almost impossible. We have seen on so many occasions how the Government opposite wants to be the judge, jury, regulator, policeman and, at the same time, the player. We have seen this in the oil and gas industry with Petro-Canada being one of the players in the game when the Government should be content to be the regulator of the oil and gas industry.
If gambling in Canada was to be privately operated, the Government could still raise a revenue from it by means of taxation. It does this already with horse racing. Look, for instance, at the state of Nevada. Nevada receives probably its greatest state revenues from the gaming industry in Las Vegas and other localities. There is no reason why the Government cannot avail itself of some of these revenue-generating opportunities.
In the past, each nation has had its own national form of ganbling. Lotteries have been commonly associated with European and South American countries. In those countries that are without a proper welfare system, the sale of lottery tickets by people who are unable to find other means of employment provide a substitute for the proper welfare payments that are available to us in Canada. In Britain, there were the soccer pools. I presume there are still soccer pools over there.

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
In Canada, our national form of gambling was always the penny stock market. I see that the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) is present, and I am sure that she would agree with me that something very useful came out of this form of gambling or speculation, and in a few moments I would like to discuss the differences between gambling and speculation. Canada created, through the development of mines financed through the issuance of penny stock, a great new wealth. Although, in many cases, the people who bought and sold these stocks did not buy them by way of investment-as far as they were concerned, they were gambling-the end result was the same. Even without dealing with penny mining stocks or penny oil stocks and dealing with other stocks or commodities that are traded in this country and others, the gambler or the speculator increases the liquidity of the market. This therefore provides an underlying economic function that we do not find with the strict gambling that is contemplated under Bill C-95.
Another argument against the lotteries that we already have in Canada and against the sports pools as contemplated in this Bill is that if we look at the figures-and I am afraid that I do not have them with me today-we will see that from the point of view of the gambler who is the person who puts his money up, the return is much better at the craps tables in Las Vegas than it is when buying provincial lottery tickets in Canada or federal lottery tickets when we had them. It seems that the Governments that run these lotteries are much too greedy and are taking off a much larger cut than they should and a much larger cut than would be allowed if the Government were the only regulator and policeman rather than also a player in the game. It seems that the Governments in the country cannot resist the temptation to milk the public for all that it is worth.
I shall say a few words now, Mr. Speaker, on Motion No. 2, which, at any rate, is the motion we are supposed to be debating. This amendment would restrict the Government, under Bill C-95, to operating only sports pools. What the Government wants to do in the present Clause 14(b)(i) is give itself blanket authority to undertake any form of gaming or gambling activity that it sees fit. I do not think that we should give the Government that blanket authority. I do not know what it would get itself into. I envisage the possibility of poker machines scattered throughout the confines of the House of Commons.
I see a distinct possibility of the federal Government returning to the lottery schemes that are run by the Provinces, and I do not think that it should want to compete with the Provinces in that type of enterprise, if that is the right word for it. We debated this subject over a period of years, and it was finally determined that lotteries should remain in the provincial domain and that the federal Government should keep out of them. I am frightened by what nefarious scheme the Government might come up with if Parliament were to grant the Government that blanket authority to undertake any form of gambling activity.
We want to restrict the effect of Bill C-95 to sports pools, as bad as they might be. We really do not know what the Government is thinking of when it talks about sports pools. It has not
told us exactly what it has in mind. I understand that it has paid many thousands of dollars to various Liberal consulting firms to dream up schemes that might be incorporated into its gambling practices. So far, it has not been forthcoming with Parliament by telling us really what it is that it wants to do.
If the Government were to adopt a scheme similar to the privately run but Government taxed soccer pools in Great Britain, the potential revenues from the operation of sports pools could be huge. I understand that in that country, many, many millions of dollars are wagered each week on the soccer pools. The Government, by this Bill, restricted as it must be to the operation of sports pools, has the possibility of generating millions of dollars worth of revenue.
In conclusion, Sir, I want to say that I support the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) in his Motion No. 2. We are giving the Government quite enough authority as it is and we cannot let it engage in any of these other nefarious schemes that it might dream up without its returning to Parliament to get more authority.

The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Concil (Mr. Smith) has spoken up about the importance of this legislation to the people of Calgary, Mr. Speaker. Why is it so much a part of the Liberal Government's approach to public policy to use and abuse Alberta, and Calgary in particular, for its partisan purposes? The Calgary Olympic Committee was formed a number of years ago and consists of citizens of Calgary, not Government, who are volunteers. They sought to bring the Winter Olympics to the City and to Canada for the first time. This seems highly appropriate. Without "big brother" providing funds, without the benefit of patronage connection to some Government, with no motive other than to provide this thrilling event for their city, their Province and their country, these citizens work hard. They sought a moral commitment of support for the games from the municipality, the provincial Government and the federal Government should they be fortunate enough to win the right for Canada. They worked for years and put together a superb package which won the approval of the International Olympic Committee.
The citizens of Calgary applauded their efforts and one would hope that the Government of Canada would also applaud their efforts and offer help to make the Olympics the show piece that they should be for Canada. Instead, we see the use of crude, political pressure. These members of the Olympic Committee, these volunteers, are trying to plan facilities and organize the games into something of which Canadians can be proud. Yet the Minister and his minions telephone them
June 27, 1983

saying, "We cannot give you any money unless we get this sports pool Bill through the House, so you had better pressure the Opposition to get it through-pressure them into agreeing to this new gambling scheme. Otherwise you will not get your money."
These volunteers continue to work. They are not out for any patronage benefit. They will not have the rights to sell these tickets and make some money, and they have not signed consulting agreements to pick up the cash that the Government bestows on its friends. They are doing all this for nothing, but they get pressure and threats. They are told, "We do not know if we are going to give you any money. It depends on the House of Commons. We told you before that we would support you and we supported the Olympics in Montreal. We made a commitment but you know we are with commitments-they mean nothing."

Mr. Speaker, I am aware that when the members of the Canadian Olympic Committee went to Baden-Baden to make their application, they carried with them a commitment of the Government of Canada to support the application for facilities. The Government is collecting money from the Loto Canada contract and it has given a commitment of support. The mechanism has nothing to do with the question. The Canadian Olympic Committee did not go before the International Olympic Committee and say, "We do not know how much support we are going to get; it depends on our stamp, coin and sports pool sales. We cannot tell how much support the federal Government will give us." They went with a commitment from the Government to support the Canadian Winter Olympics.
No other city in Canada would be so used and abused, Mr. Speaker. No other group of volunteers would be so used and abused the way the Calgary group is. It seems to be a part of the system. Whether we are dealing with the Olympics or anything else, it is acceptable to the Government to use that king of crude pressure. It is especially hard to take when it is talked about in the same breath as national unity and important symbols.
If the Minister is sincere in saying that the interest of the federal Government in the sports pool is solely to help the Calgary Olympics in 1988, then he will agree with Motion No. 2 to strike out Clause 14(6) which extends the legislation far beyond what he just mentioned. It says that the Governor in
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
Council can open up any form of lawful gaming activity as a source of revenue for whatever purpose the Government wants. If the Minister is sincere, let him accept the motion, strike out Clause 14(6) and restrict the Bill to the sports pool. If he is sincere, he will accept Motions Nos. 2 and 3 and restrict this to the Winter Olympics. That would prove his sincerity, but I do not think it is likely to happen.
Some of my colleagues have raised the question of the morality of the Government of Canada asking for the right to do what we do not think Canadian citizens have the right to do, namely, to run gambling establishments, run a gaming house, to exploit the human weakness of trying to get rich for nothing and to make money without providing goods or services. It offers the allure of gambling. If we were sincere and honest we would recognize that as a human weakness and not something to be encouraged and exploited by Government any more than other human weaknesses should be exploited for the benefit of Government.
It has been said that the reality of the situation is that taxes on gambling are a tax on the poor, and the data confirms that. There are those who do not have a lot and who hope to achieve their dream through a lottery ticket or a sports pool. Surely it is a sad situation when the Government of Canada sees an opportunity for revenue in this. It is revenue which has a real attractiveness in the political sense because it can be used for patronage purposes by granting the right to sell tickets to our friends by all of these contracts which have been talked about. It is money which, strictly speaking, does not go through the Consolidated Revenue Fund as do other tax dollars. It is money which can be used for really nice political purposes to help "us" get re-elected. That is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is just plain immoral. The Calgary Olympics will succeed because of the Calgarians who are working on it, managing it and putting it together. It will succeed. It will be an outstanding success in spite of this Minister's attempt to undermine the confidence and the support which this group requires.

anything good in it, anything which I could accept, or anything which made any sense at all. Regretfully, I could find absolutely nothing in this legislation except that it made me feel somewhat embarrassed that this country could have such a Government which would deliberately, maliciously and viciously go in for living off the poor and living off gambling.
At the moment, Ontario residents are the biggest lottery spenders per capita in Canada, the fourth largest in North America. They spend an average now of $63.95 per person a year on lotteries. That is more than double the amount for the rest of Canada where the average spending is somewhere about $30 per person. I am even wondering if in my own Province of British Columbia, people understand that there is between $70 million and $80 million a year which flows through lotteries. I am not against an individual who wants to make a bet with the guy at the next desk over the hockey game on a particular evening. That is a simple transaction between two consenting adults. Neither one of them is going to be hurt. However, when you institutionalize the sports pool, and you ask people to select the winners of ten games-and that is really what a sports pool is, similar to the English pools-that is not what I would see as showing the ability of someone to select who is going to win and who is going to lose because they are experts in a particular sport. If you multiply the permutations which are involved in picking 10 or 12 games, you are buying a lottery ticket and that is all you are buying. It is just another lottery, regardless of what it is called.
We now have this nonsense about support of the Calgary Olympics. You can always trust the Liberals to find a red herring somewhere, or somewhere to trans-affect what is really taking place. From what I can gather, this Government could not care less about the Calgary Olympics, but it is a nice excuse to hang this fraud upon the Canadian people. "The Calgary Olympics do not get the money unless we get our sports pool", is what is implied. That is supposed to make those of us from western Canada very careful of what we say about this rather unfortunate legislation. We are supposed to lie down and pretend that, by golly, Calgary has to have support and this is the only way to get it. The Government of Canada must support the Olympic Games. I believe it is true in Ontario, and I believe even in Quebec the Liberals will find that Canadians want the Calgary Olympics fully supported by their national Government.
Let me give a little history now, and I suppose a bit of "mea culpa". I can remember in the early 1960s when a little lady by the name of Mary English in the City of Calgary became very excited about Canada's lottery laws. She found some support, raised some money, made a pilgrimage to Ottawa, appeared on radio stations, and gave interviews right across this country. I do not know where you are now, Mary, but I know this much, that I am sorry I supported you. I did not realize what was going to happen if her campaign succeeded, which it did, quite frankly. It changed the thinking of Canadian people about lotteries. So that today we have a situation where we now have super loto. It costs $10 per ticket. That is not what Mary English had in mind. Ten dollars is a lot of money. A few $10 bills put together buys an awful lot of things. When you multiply it by hundreds and hundreds, it is a
significant portion of Canada's national product. For the winners there is $1 million. However, the odds are about
800,000	to one. The provincial lottery is $5 per ticket. The top prize is $500,000. Again, the chances are 800,000 to one. Wintario-there is something for everyone in the lottery field-is $1 per ticket. Top prize is $100,000. The odds are a million to one. Lottario costs $1 per ticket. The odds-you should not buy "Lottario"-are 3.2 million to one. Cash for life costs $2 per ticket. The top prize is $50,000 per year for life. The odds are 1.4 million to one. The Pot of Gold costs $2 per ticket. The top prize is $100,000. The odds are one million to one. Then there is Loto 649. If that is not close to what we are proposing with the sports pool, then I do not know what is. It costs $1 per ticket. The top prize is $1 million. The odds are, believe it or not, 13,983,806 to one. What do you suppose the odds are going to be on anyone actually cashing a sports pool ticket? The odds are going to be astronomical because it is a numbers game. Picking that many games is almost an impossibility.
What really has disturbed me about this legislation is the lack of protest in the country. I have always believed that people get the Governments they deserve, with perhaps the exception of the Canadian people in the last three years. Where has the massive protest from the recreational industry of Canada been? Do they not realize that when people are buying these ruddy tickets, those dollars are going into something where there is no real output in terms that make sense for their industry? There have been some protests from the churches. Reverend Much more, where are you when we really need you badly? We certainly can use you on this rediculous legislation which is being proposed. Where is the massive protest? Some have protested, but not nearly as many as should.
Where is the moral indignation of the Canadian people at a Government which will foist this on them? I believe part of the answer is that there is no doubt that this particular bit of legislation is likely to be "steamrollered" through. This Government is going to force this upon us whether we like it or not. That is rather unfortunate because I think that if its Members listened to some of the speeches here, as I have this afternoon, and some of the other speeches which are going to be made, it would find that a good many of them make a good deal of sense in terms of modifying this Bill or finding reasons why this legislation should not be passed. Unfortunately, the problem with the Government is that once it does something, it is like a brick wall and you can never get it to change. Even if it thought it was wrong, it would not admit it. That is what bugs me about this legislation-it is wrong. It is wrong for the Canadian people. It is not as if Canadians did not have access to a lottery ticket, a home grown lottery ticket, if you like. They do now, in several areas, and at tremendous odds. For those persons who want a lottery ticket, fine, they can buy one. But to foist this one additional sport pool lottery on top of anything else and, I might add, to change the law in such a
June 27, 1983

way that it totally opens the door for other Ministers to play with this thing, to expand gambling in Canada in a variety of ways, doing it by Order-in-Council without ever having to come to the House again or to ever have it publicly debated properly in the House of Commons is, to me, the most dangerous feature about this particular legislation and the proposed changes to the Code.
1 will be voting against it, of course. I will be voting against the Government all the way on this one, and talking about it in years to come. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member. In principle, I do not believe in gambling. Anyone who has been in the army, for instance, has seen it take place excessively. Anyone who has worked in the woods camp knows that for an orderly, peaceful woods operation one does not play poker. Anyone who has been associated with the Legion in this country after World War II knows that. An attempt was made after the war to extend to members of the Legion the opportunity to continue some of their former habits, one of which was gambling. Anyone who has been associated with a branch of the Legion is aware of the fact that in virutally every instance, the gambling opportunity had to be removed. Everyone knows that service clubs have tried on several occasions to raise some of their funds for their requirements with slot machines. They have found that in the main their members went broke. While the club became rich, the members went broke; some of them, not all of them, because not all people are compulsive gamblers.
The Bill, therefore, is absolutely contradictory to the principles which would support a moral operation of the Olympic
Athletic Contests and Events Pooh Act
games in Canada. That is the first point. My principles tell me that this is a dead wrong and immoral act by the Government of Canada to try to exploit the gambling instincts of the people of Canada to fulfil an international obligation as well as a local obligation in Canada. Let us deal with the international obligation.
There are nations which are involved in a treaty type of agreement with respect to the conduct of Olympic games in this world. Any application received from any country in the world is accompanied by a recommendation from the responsible Government and, in the case of the federal Government of Canada, an indication that there will be fiscal responsibility. Oh, yes, Mr. Speaker, and without that inherent guarantee and the recommendation of the Government concerned no Olympic game would be extended to any country.
There was another little hassle over a very comparable measure in the House before the present Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) became a Member of the House of Commons. In the consultations and considerations with respect to the financing of the Olympic games in Montreal it was made very clear to the committee that the favourable recommendation of the Government of Canada for the Summer Olympics in Montreal certainly included a guarantee of fiscal capability. That guarantee was given by the Government of Canada.
The Minister may shake his head but I ask him, before he opens his mouth after shaking his head, to explore the standards by which the International Olympic Committee will extend the privilege of conducting games in any country in the world. The national Government's recommendation and support are inherent to the guarantee of fiscal responsibility.
Therefore, it is not playing perfectly honestly with the people of Canada, at best, to say, "Oh, the Government of Canada must have this Bill through by June 30". It is quite improper to say that; it is deceptive. That approach to the Olympic Committee of Calgary, to the Olympic Committee of Canada and to the athletes of Canada is absolutely and utterly ignoring the absolute guarantee of financial responsibility which was included in and interpreted as such a guarantee when the Government's support for the application went before the international committee that allocated the games. That is the first point.
Second, for any Minister of the Government of Canada to say to any local committee that it shall be financed for the sponsoring of these games in a particular way and only in a particular way is (a) a threat to the sponsors of Calgary and (b) a breach of the international obligation which this nation look on.
I want to say to Your Honour that anyone in this nation who thinks there is anything but a threat to the Olympic athletes, the Olympic Committee and the city of Calgary had better become familiarized with the terms and conditions, on an international basis, under which the Government became responsible.

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
I do not like deceptive methods. Yes, the Minister responsible for sports did, in fact, dissolve one loto set up by the Government of Canada. This was in fact returned to the authority to which it belonged, namely, the Provinces. When there is a mere $90 billion budget in the nation, to say to the people of Canada that we must have a loto and exploit the gamblers of Canada to finance the athletic games which will be conducted in 1988 is deception at a disgustingly low level.
I do not favour lotteries in a public sence because of the exploitation of the compulsive gambler to the detriment of his family's well being. After all the lessons learned about the impact upon the family welfare of the compulsive gambler, for the Government of Canada to be bringing in this kind of legislation is contempt of its moral responsibility.
There was an offer made to the Government. Why did it not take it up? Why did the Government not take up the voluntary offer of the provincially conducted lotteries in this nation to conduct a special program to finance the Calgary deal? Why does the Government want to get into every aspect of gambling available to mankind by the permissive legislation it is trying to get us to pass and which we are trying to amend? I hope this nation understands the outright deceit the Government is placing before athletes in Calgary and this nation as it tries to boondoggle the House into the necessity of passing this legislation; it told Calgary that it can only give it what it can get from a lottery. That is simply horseradish.
It is most difficult to understand what has happened to all those voluntary groups in the country which used to put baseball, hockey and other athletic teams together as a community effort. People were prepared to put money forward in their community to support those endeavours. Ever since the initial introduction of lotteries in Canada, those same organizations ask how much they can get from the Government whether provincial or federal. Why should they raise money? Why should there be an interest in the community any longer to try to field these teams which contribute so much to the communities? Why should they build a tennis court or a rink? Lotteries have had a very derogatory effect upon the initiative in communities of Canada since Government moneys have been allocated on a political basis from a gambling organization to support this type of event.
In principle, I denounce this Bill, and I doubly denounce the deceptive way it is being presented to Canadians. I feel sorry for misled Calgarians who believe they will only have the Olympic Games if there is a lottery. That is a downright disgraceful and deceitful proposition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity today to speak against this particular Bill. Normally, I would relish the thought of making comments on a Government or an Opposition Bill, but I find this Bill particularly distasteful for a number of reasons. One is the link which has been made between this Bill and the Calgary Olympics. I want to say here and now that I and my Party obviously support the Olympics being held in one of our
finest cities in western Canada. I am sure that all Members of the House are proud of Canada's athletes and the fact that we will host this competition, inviting athletes from around the world. We wish them the greatest success. We also support fitness and sports in general. We support the concept of fitness, recreation and other leisure activities.
However, the Government has given the impression that those who speak against this Bill also speak against the idea of the Olympics and fitness and health in general. That is absolutely false. As Opposition Members, we are trying to say in the House today that we are in favour of those activities but opposed to this Bill.
This Bill proposes to provide money for activities such as the Calgary Olympics, arts and culture in Canada, fitness and amateur sports, medical and health research and worthy capital projects. These	are all	projects	which I believe allMembers of the House	strongly	support.	They are all	worthy
of the appropriate support from the federal Government, along with other levels of Government.
However, we feel very strongly that these worthwhile endeavours should not be funded on the backs of Canada's poor. If these are legitimate activities-there is no question that they are-they should be funded from general revenues, so that those who are able to pay, do so. The taxes and moneys for these worth while	endeavours can	be collected	in anequitable fashion from	our tax	system;	the myth of	course
being that our tax system is equitable and fair, and that is an entirely different matter, but at least it is the basis upon which we have a so-called progressive tax system in our country. If these are worthwhile endeavours, let us fund them properly from the general tax base in Canada and not by a gambling cassino approach to health, fitness, amateur sports, culture and arts and the Olympics.
This Bill institutionalizes gambling in this country. It sets up a gambling business on a permanent basis, endorsed by the federal Governemnt of Canada. Imagine the message being sent to Canadians from all walks of like and all regions at a time when they are desperately looking to the federal Government for leadership and direction. These are confusing and difficult times at best. The people of this country are looking to their national and regional leaders for advice. What advice is the Government of Canada giving to Canadians? It is telling them to gamble. It believes the answer to funding some of the most worthwhile endeavours in our country is to set up a gambling cassino so that all Canadians can gamble. That is the message being conveyed by the Government.
I am one of those Members of the House of Commons who does not believe that people should gamble as a way out of an economic dilemma. Gambling is not the answer to obtaining the necessary cash flow for individuals, their families or communities. I suggest the Government is providing poor leadership when it encourages people to pull $5, $20, or $100 bills from their pockets to participate in this federal Government gambling business. What sort of message does a Bill like this send to the people of Canada?
June 27, 1983

If we believe in amateur sports and fitness, in arts and culture, medical and health research, is it not time we began spending money collected from legitimate sources, using legitimate methods, as opposed to asking people to get rich quick by gambling? Perhaps that is good Liberal advice because it falls in with Liberal economic planning. I have always considered the Liberal approach to economic planning as being the Las Vegas school of economics; go out and gamble on the longshot. Of course, the longshot for the Liberal Government was called the megaprojects in western Canada or, more precisely, the energy projects. That was the Liberals' gamble. If the card they played had been the right one at the right time they would be laughing. The funds would be rolling in and all of the programs, the porkbarrelling and patronage would be flowing in all directions and they would be well off electorally as well as economically. However, the gamble did not pay off. All the eggs in that one basket called the megaprojects in western Canada failed because the right card did not come out.
The Liberal Government is now asking Canadians to use that same mentality. It is telling the average citizen of Canada who is struggling to make ends meet, the average small-business person, the farmers, the ranchers and fishermen of Canada who are struggling to establish their families' cash flow, to follow the Government's great idea to buy these tickets and spend their hard earned money because they might strike it rich. It says that they should not feel badly if they do not strike it rich because the money they invest will be used to pay for such things as medical research and the development of arts and culture in Canada.
This Bill is almost laughable. It is a sad comment when we see Ministers standing up during these tragic economic times to say that this is the answer to funding these worth while endeavours. Their answer is to turn Canadians into gamblers and Canada into one large Las Vegas. We in the NDP believe this is exactly the wrong approach. This is not the right step. This is a program that has not been thought through carefully. If it is a well thought out program 1 should like to hear Members opposite stand up and condone gambling; say that gambling is the best interests of the country, that gambling is in the best interests of our economy and in the best interests of arts, culture, amateur sport and fitness and so on.
In closing, let me say with disgust that this kind of approach to economic development, to the funding of the arts, sciences, sports and fitness is a sad proposal put forward by the Government of Canada; it is a sad proposal. The only thing I can say is that as Opposition Members we will be doing what we can to voice our opposition, and to try to bring the Government to some sense. There are much better ways to fund these worthwhile ventures, such as the Calgary Olympics, than turning the nation into one national set of Las Vegas players.

1 would like to suggest to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap that lotteries have existed for a long time in some form or another in every community across this country. There are turkey raffles, car raffles, and car bingos. These are all a form of lottery. It is quite accepted that this is the way money is raised in communities to build parks, swimming pools and other things. As a former Kinsman and a former Rotarian, we did a number of these things for the good of the community. People knew what they were doing. People recognized the odds against them when they bought those lottery tickets.
The Hon. Member, like the rest of the NDP, says "no, that is wrong. Even though you want to do it you cannot do it because we know best. We will dictate to you and we will lay it out because it is morally wrong", or whatever. I do not take exception to the lottery system if that is what the people want. People have always bought lottery tickets. They buy tickets when a car is raffled, when a cake is raffled, when coins are raffled, or whatever. It is done in virtually every community of our nation. That is fine if that is what the people want to do, I believe in freedom for those people to do that.
I take considerable exception to this Government bringing in Bill C-95 at this time. It is sleazy, underhanded and wrong; not because it is another lottery but because an agreement was signed with the Provinces stating on behalf of the federal Government, "We will not enter into the lottery system." This Government took it to the courts for a legal opinion. That legal opinion received by the Minister was that the federal Government could not go into lotteries because that process had been signed away to the Provinces.
Let us look at what the Government is doing. From 1979 the federal Government was to get $24 million a year for doing absolutely nothing but leaving the jurisdiction of the lottery system and lottery games in the hands and the purview of the Provinces. This $24 million a year the Government got for doing absolutely nothing was tied to the Consumer Price Index. This year it looks like the federal Government will receive $32 million in revenue. Since the agreement was signed the federal Government has received close to $100 million for doing absolutely nothing except allowing the Provinces to control the lotteries.
The provinces are better able to protect against abuse, and better able to run the lottery system. But the federal Government has seen the potential revenue it might receive. The federal Governments now uses the argument that it takes skill to pick certain winners and therefore this system is no longer a lottery. The Government saw the possible loophole in relation to sports pools. The federal Government knew full well that the then Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport and

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some trepidation to speak on Bill C-95. Perhaps I could first make a remark about the reformed rules of the House. I trust by the end of the year we will have looked very hard at the idea of sitting here from eleven o'clock in the morning until eleven o'clock at night. I know this has nothing to do with the Bill before the House; it is simply a bind in which we all seem to be when we are foolish enough to sentence ourselves to these hours for the month of June.
This Bill authorizes gambling. It authorizes any type or description of gambling which in future years suits the Cabinet. There are many people who should never gamble. Unfortunately most gamblers come from poorer sections of the community. They can least afford it but seem most addicted to it. When I was a youngster my very first experience with gambling was when I attended the Yorkton Fair in Saskatchewan. I was a kid off the farm. My Dad gave me a dollar for the whole day to spend on rides, for admission into the exhibition grounds, the grandstand and everything. He gave it to me at 8.30 in the morning and I was back home at 9.00, an hour later. I had found one of those wheels which went tick, tick, tick; the lights flashed and I lost my dollar. My Dad said, "a fool and his money are soon parted". His name was Peter MacDonald McKinnon; he did not part with dollars lightly.
June 27, 1983

There are what used to be called gentlemanly forms of gambling. For example, a person could play bridge with people of equal talent. If he was not of equal talent, it would dawn on him sooner or later and he could withdraw. But the type of gambling which the Government is now encouraging is addictive. People tend to get into debt over it.
We saw an example of a female accountant in a firm in Toronto the other day who had managed to get away with a couple of hundred thousand dollars. When asked what she had done with it she said she had spent it on lottery tickets because she was convinced she would win some day. As I have travelled the world I have noticed that there is a connection between the moral fibre of a country, the prosperity of a country and the amount of lottery tickets which are sold. I have travelled through western European countries, Britain, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt, Mexico, United States and Canada.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT

speechtext: And what about Britain?

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT

speechtext: I believe there is a pretty close connection between poverty and government authorized or approved gambling. I hear the Minister asking me about Britain. One did not bet ten pounds per week on the pools; one bet ten pence. Even so, in the poorer parts of the country more people were selling pool tickets and gambling on contrived methods. Pools are not entirely gambling. There is a certain amount of knowledge and at those levels there is very little in the way of broken homes or people spending their grocery money. But the situation is different here with a type of gambling where everyone is asked to operate as if it were a numbers game. For most people who purchase tickets it will be a numbers game.

Generally the people who play the British pools are very skilled at estimating soccer scores. If the Minister is to obtain the amount of money he hopes for, he has to appeal to people who do not have any more notion on what they are betting than when they buy lottery tickets and watch the bit on television with coloured balls to discover the winners. This is a form of regressive taxation of the worst kind, and there can be no doubt about it. The term "regressive" used in this sense means a taxation which hits hardest those people who can least afford it. I suspect if the Minister conducted a pool among people in the House, for instance, he would find there is very little purchasing of tickets, because most of us are not poor and have enough wits to realize what a bad investment it would be to purchase a lottery ticket hoping to win any money.
Since I lost that first dollar I must admit that I have gambled a fair amount, but usually 1 had a better chance of winning than 1 would have here. A person can always cover his gambling urges by saying that he is investing in the country or in resource industries. I have done my share of that. Sometimes he wins; sometimes he buys Dome Petroleum thinking
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
that it might pay off. If anyone here wishes to buy shares of Dome Petroleum I have quite a few I would be willing to sell at cost. The losers, though, will be the Canadian people and the winner will be the Canadian government. But with its usual way of doing things, I suspect the Government will turn a winner into a loser. Recently someone said that if we gave the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) the Sahara Desert, in six months they would have to import sand. That is the kind of skill they have in these natural things. 1 recall a former Minister, Iona Campagnola, who was in early on the lottery fiasco. She managed to sign a contract before she brought it to the House and got into all kinds of trouble. I suppose that showed some kind of Party loyalty, for now she is the President of the Liberal Party. Those things could only happen in the Liberal Party.
I would like to turn to the amendment that is being considered at the moment. Let me point out one of the clauses in this boondoggle which will become a statute. It reads:
One of the directors appointed ... shall be designated by the Governor in Council as Chairman and the Board shall select the Vice-Chairman from among the other such directors.
This leaves it up to the Government to appoint these people. We know from previous experience what kind of people they appoint to Government boards. As usual, they will be high-salaried and incompetent. What I worry about, and the amendment speaks of it, is the types of gaming that will be carried on. It appears to me that anything at all will be allowed.
Let us look at one of the Government's recent investments in a public corporation, Petro-Canada. Once this Bill is passed, I expect that the Government will be able to allow a poker game to take place in the back room of every PetroCanada station in this country. There will be a civil servant there taking what is commonly called the "rake-off'. With most gambling, the size of the rake-off dictates whether a person should get into it or not. The rake-off on some of these games will be large indeed because this Bill permits it.
The disbursements have a peculiar tinge to them. I notice in the Bill that some of these disbursements are for good causes. However, others are a little odd. On page 8 of the Bill it states:
There shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to or for the support of any one or more of
(a) activities in the following fields:
(i)	the arts and culture,
(ii)	fitness and amateur sport, and
(iii)	medical and health research.
This reference to medical and health research is interesting. It could entail a great deal of money if the Government is going to seriously approach funding for health research. However, it further states in paragraph (c)
-worthy capital projects of national interest in the fields described in Subparagraphs (a)(i) and (ii).

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
That refers to arts and culture and fitness and amateur sport, but not medical and health research. One becomes curious as to how they will become selective as they go through this process. In one paragraph certain things will be funded and in the next paragraph the funding will be cancelled. Clause 21 reads:
The accounts and financial transactions of the Corporation shall be audited each year by an auditor appointed by the Governor in Council for a term not exceeding three years.
I certainly do not agree with that. We on this side are convinced the Auditor General and not Cabinet-appointed auditors, should audit Crown corporations.
Clause 14 is the one that the amendment speaks to. I quote paragraph (d):
The objects of the Corporation are-
(b) to conduct and manage, in accordance with regulations made by the Governor in Council, such lawful gaming activities as the Governor in Council directs.
As I said before, that is a kind of open sesame to all kinds of gambling.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment before us deletes Clause 14(l)(b) which reads:
-to conduct and manage, in accordance with regulations made by the Governor in Council, such lawful gaming activities as the Governor in Council directs.
This Bill is not about a sports pool. Is it about the Government making lawful such gaming activities as it decides are proper. Aside from the question of lotteries, pools, Olympics and sports, this is an authority by the Governor in Council, the Cabinet, to authorize all sorts of gambling activities, activities not even yet devised. On that basis alone, this Bill should fail.
I am glad the Minister is in the chamber. I want him to hear what happened to a relative of mine who was working for a major trust company in Ontario. She decided to dip into the till and falsify the records of that trust company to buy Lottario tickets and tickets on Olympic lotteries at one time run by this Government. She was very clever at it. She managed to get into that trust company to the extent of $45,000 before an audit revealed what had happened. As a result of arrangements, she did not go to jail; nor was she prosecuted. Something was done to look after her, but that did not stop her. She again got a job of trust and was able to get into her next employer to the extent of some $17,000. She felt that if the Government was going to run a lottery system, it must be good and it must be a fair system. Therefore, she could get back all the things she had taken from people and replace her losses by one of those winnings. She was going to be the one in a million winner. She was going to be independently wealthy. She was going to have the hopes and dreams that she had wanted simply because the Government was promising them to her in television ad campaigns.
An article appeared in The Globe and Mail with respect to gambling. I want to read into the record a statement made by Dr. Robert Politzer, Director of the Johns Hopkins University,
Pathological Gambling Counselling sector at Mount Wilson near Baltimore. He said and I quote:
Not his family, not his job, nothing. He becomes driven to the point of breaking laws to get the money he needs to gamble. Gambling, not the winning or losing of money, becomes an end to itself.
In the practice of law I had the opportunity to handle a great number of clients in business. One was a young man who came from Yugoslavia. He had built up a very successful contracting business. When I first got to know him he owned several small appartment buildings that he had built. He managed to put together a door company in Mississauga which made fire-resistant doors. He had several pieces of attractive land on which he was speculating.
This man was on his way to becoming a millionaire, if he was not already there. Then he found out about the ponies and about gambling. He was one of those, roughly one in one hundred, persons in our society who is compulsive in gambling. He went bankrupt. His marriage went bankrupt and his family went bankrupt.
To have a Government of this country come before this House and say in the interest of sports, the Olympics, culture of all things, it is going to trade on the disease, the compulsiveness of some of its citizens who will wind up with destroyed families, who will wind up taking advantage as my relative did of the promise by a Government to make them wealthy, is wrong and must be opposed by every right-thinking person in this House. This Bill must appal the very basic conscience of every Member of the House on the basis of individual knowledge. It does not take very much experience living in a society like ours to know that there are members of society who do not buy one ticket but buy ten tickets or 20 tickets, who buy tickets with money that is not their own, who dip into the till. One does not have to be a criminal lawyer to defend that type of person because that type of person can be a member of one's own family.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when this Minister brings forth this kind of a Bill, he ought to be ashamed of himself. This Government has an obligation to finance Olympic activities on behalf of us all. That money can come from various sources of Government revenue, from income tax to corporate tax to duties and customs. But surely the Government ought not to trade on the incapacity of some people to resist games of chance. To present a Bill that deliberately allows the Cabinet to authorize other forms of gambling behind this corporation must repel us all. It must be the kind of thing that a Government interested in criminal law, morality and the right thing would tear up in disgust. Yet the Minister says: "Oh, well, you must have it. If you want to finance these things, we must have a slush fund." Well, I say to him that if his need for a slush fund is that great, the Government is all slush and no principle. It will be defeated, if not on this Bill, then by the general public of the country in an election.
June 27, 1983

Mr. Speaker, in joining my colleagues in opposing Bill C-95, I find that there are a number of provisions in the Bill which, from a practical and moral standpoint, have not been addressed by the Government in committee. The proposals now before the House are not acceptable.
The two major practical objections to the Bill are the unsound economics of the proposed Bill and the inclusion of Clause 14(b) which we are now discussing, and which will be seriously detrimental to the setting up of the sports pool. Let me refer for a moment to the economic unsoundness of the Bill.
The Hon. Reuben Baetz, Minister of Tourism and Recreation for Ontario, appeared before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture on December 16, 1982. As a shareholder of the Interprovincial Lottery Corporation and as their Chairman for the last four years, he is well informed about the mechanics of running a lottery. As one who had a part in setting up the first Manitoba Lottery when I was Executive Director of the Manitoba Centennial Corporation, I was particularly interested in his comments and the overview he brought to the committee. At one point, he stated categorically:
I am here today to tell you that the federal Government sports pool cannot generate the levels of profit that have been suggested by the federal Government.
The reasons for the sports pool's undoubted failure have been well presented by my colleagues previously in this debate.
[ Translation]
We know that sports pools represent a very small percentage of the market. For instance, if we look at the Province of Quebec and its Hockey Select lottery, we find that the percentage of ticket sales for hockey sports pools has been decreasing regularly.

Not only is there the drop suggested in expected revenue. We have been told that the sports pool will collect $30 million to $40 million a year. Mr. Baetz, when appearing before committee, suggested that this amount will not be enough to even cover the cost of the equipment needed to run the game. We have a $10.5 million start-up grant that is not even expected to be recovered and, as we were told in Committee, an estimated $20 million that will be borrowed. That makes $30.5 million. The moneys generated would not come anywhere near covering the $200 million the Government has promised Calgary for the Olympics.
Second, the motion proposed by the Official Opposition would strike Clause 14(b). This Clause is unnecessary to the running of the sports pools and is potentially harmful to our relations with the Provinces. It gives the federal Government the authority to conduct and manage, in accordance with regulations made by the Governor in Council, such lawful gaming activities as the Governor in Council directs. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? We are told that it is not the Government's intention to get back into the lottery business. If
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
not, what other kinds of lawful gaming activities will we see- video games, national bingo games, Trivial Pursuit on national television?
The Provinces, very rightly, I believe, mistrust this Clause. If it is not removed, the Provinces will be very unco-operative in establishing this sports pool. As officials of the Provinces have said again and again, they do not like the idea of negotiating with a gun to their heads. They feel it threatens the agreement made between the federal and provincial Governments in August of 1979 whereby the Provinces have paid to the Government about $34 million a year in exchange for having the federal Government withdraw from the lottery business. Clause 14(b), the Mack truck Clause, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), so aptly puts it, seriously jeopardizes the spirit of mutual trust that is so essential for future negotiations.
Let me then look at the practical applications of the Bill and summarize three other objections I have in the practical sphere. First, as my colleague pointed out a few moments ago, there is the possibility of political patronage. A second objection is that it is relatively easy to fix a sports game as compared to other forms of lotteries. Therefore, the Government is taking a risk entering into this area. Third, the beneficiary structure is too large and too vague. We have no clear advance idea of how the Calgary Olympics will benefit as opposed to fitness and amateur sports, health and medical research, arts and culture, to say nothing of the specification of worthy capital projects.
I would like to make some comments in relation to the objections I have on moral grounds. I do so in relation to my own convictions and also in relation to my responsibility as Opposition critic of the Minister of the Secretary of State, a ministry directed to encouraging wholesome citizenship. I see nothing in the Government's decision to go hand in hand with the promotion of lotteries that will encourage a healthly sense of citizenship in Canada.
I, along with other Members, today received a representation made by the Reverend Robert G. Lindsey, Senior Staff Officer of Church in Society for the United Church of Canada. The representation he makes to Canadians and to the House of Commons is as follows:
This is the time to stop further Government promotion of gambling in Canada. The United Church of Canada is concerned with the Government's refusal to understand its obligation to support morality in Canada rather than to undermine it. We hope that you will do whatever is in your power to stop Bill C-195 from becoming law in Canada.
I received a similar representation dated June 24 from Rev. A. G. Van Eek of the Council of Christian Reformed Churches in Canada. He outlines the concern of that constituency about lotteries which raise or capitalize upon false hopes and that worthy projects are somehow put in jeopardy. He also suggests that they take up the disposable income of low-income earners, and for these reasons and others he suggests that it is not in the interests of Canada to continue.

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
I believe that lotteries are an undue celebration of chance. Others who have spoken before the committee who are not in any way prudish and who do not wish to remove fun and opportunity for Canadians see this as undercutting an important fabric.
Prof. McCormack Smyth of York University says:
Liberal democratic government has been based on a number of central ideas. One is that government must respect human beings. Governments must not exploit human weaknesses. Through their promotion of lotteries, governments are appealing to one of the lowest human qualities, that of greed. Lotteries promote, albeit unconsciously, the view that it is in order for individuals to be their brother's taker.
Because someone is willing to be taken is no excuse for exploiting that person. Public support for an idea does not make it right, as was demonstrated by child labour, slavery and racial discrimination. 1 think that gambling is proportionately more harmful to poor people than it is to people in high-income brackets. The net effect of lotteries and their acceleration is to warp public direction. I therefore join with my colleagues in opposing this legislation which is in conflict with other areas of Government direction.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to make a few comments in opposition to Bill C-95. The Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) has expressed his views very well and has given no useful references. Others who made representation to the committee were concerned with the principles involved with this type of legislative proposal to bring to Canadians a regressive taxation. It is a little like the photo opportunity of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde)-they do not really understand it but they are co-operating and assisting the Government in an indirect taxation that in many cases will do them harm.
The Bill represents a number of shades in a number of areas. It has gone from what I would consider the traditional Liberal red into a very grey area. It clouds a number of principles involved in federalism, democracy and participatory Government.
The first area is the commitment of several hundred million that the federal Government made to the Calgary Olympics. To use this legislation as a guise for fulfilling that commitment is not only questionable because of the undetermined profitability of the Bill, but it is also a back door approach to raising the revenues expected as a result of that commitment.
The second grey area is the whole concept of federal-provincial agreements. Relations are already strained and have been for several years on such things as the energy Bill and the Constitution. In this instance, an agreement was made with the Provinces that they would have exclusive domain over lotteries. Now there is a grand argument about whether the sports pool is a lottery. I understand that the courts may not find in favour of the federal Government. That may not be a major factor in determining whether the sports pool goes forward but it brings to light the federal-provincial agreements that should be honoured by the federal Government if we are to expect to
have co-operation and confidence between Governments in the future.
The third point that many speakers have referred to is the ethics and the morality of this measure. From time to time most of us participate in events related to gambling, whether through buying a lottery ticket, playing Crown and Anchor at an amusement park or some charitable fund raising event. What we have before us is on a very different level, however. The federal Government, the highest institution in the country, is sending a signal to people who are vulnerable, who are potentially compulsive gamblers. We may be promoting a potential disease by this kind of thing whether in the young, the old, or those who are unable to meet their commitments and who become too involved in this type of activity.
Recently a newspaper published the ratio of opportunities to win. Loto Canada gives one chance to win in 600,000. The odds in other lotteries are worse and the opportunity to win can be one in several million. People who participate in this class of activity can dream of being the one person in 600,000 who will win, but participation can create a problem for a family on a rigid budget. As a federal Government we have an obligation to try to avoid promoting this participation.
The fourth grey area is that of Government revenue. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) spoke about regressive taxation. It must be made clear to Canadians that the Government is raising revenue through this type of activity and that it plans to distribute the revenue to activities that all of us would support. It is a means of raising Government revenues. It is not called taxation but it really is taxation and it is often collected from those least able to afford it.
The fifth grey area is federal Crown corporations. We might have a little more confidence in this particular Crown corporation if we had not seen some of the difficulties encountered by previous Crown corporations involved in the lottery business. It is clear that very bad decisions were made. It is a complex and very precise type of activity which requires all of the resources of Government, or whoever is involved, to make sure it is done properly. There are some good examples of extreme waste in running the lotteries. I do not believe anyone in particular, in light of the recent events on the Canadian national scene, can have confidence that this Crown corporation is going to be run any better than any of the other Crown corporations. That, I feel, gives us cause for concern. The whole problem of Cana-dair is the kind of thing which points to the question of whether or not the Government, and the Minister who is responsible, are going to be able to keep up to the management requirements and whether they are going to be able to make the necessary changes in time to avoid abuse and waste which will occur if we are not right on top of it.
The sixth point, which is important, is the question of disbursements of the profits, whatever those profits might be. It is clear there has been a commitment made to the Calgary Olympics. I am sure that all Hon. Members are supportive of the Government honouring that commitment. Beyond that,
June 27, 1983

however, there is a list of what this amendment, which is being proposed at this time, would do. In fact, it would limit the disbursement of these funds to the Calgary Olympics. It would not give the Government the option of disbursing these funds to other areas which are defined, and which may not in fact be defined specifically in the Bill.
I feel the question which arises here, and the grey area, is what happens to these areas, for instance, medical research, when we have a situation where it becomes dependent upon a sports pool and then, all of a sudden, we find, as is happening in Quebec, that the returns are diminishing. There is less and less money available. We would have what to me is a very credible and worth-while project gradually being put in a position where it is very vulnerable because there are not the funds which were anticipated. Therefore, that puts these projects at high risk.
I will probably have an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, as further amendments are brought forward, to make additional comments. However, I feel that I should emphasize again that in spite of supporting most of the activities which the Government is suggesting in this legislation, it seems to be a very poor vehicle, one which has more problems than solutions, and we would like to see the Government withdraw it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments to comment on this Bill. It is the kind of Bill which the Government has put forward as a necessity. The Government is saying in effect, "If we do not get this money in this way, we will not have the money to do a lot of these wonderful things which are important for the country." One of the real criticisms of our modern age has been the so-called loss of the moral approach to living. Morality is the fibre of the nation which must be recognized and held dear at all levels. We teach it in the home, we teach it in the schools, we teach it in the church. We hope that it becomes part of every person's way of dealing with life. Then, by a variety of means, our teachings on morality are diverted in such a way that it is difficult for the nation to say, "What you are doing is wrong".
A couple of thousands of years ago the collection of interest was considered immoral and probably today it still is. However, our society has condoned it for so long that we now think of it as quite acceptable. At one time the idea of speculation was considered immoral. If one went out and bought land, for instance, for $1 an acre and sold it for $1,000 an acre a few months later, that was considered immoral. Even excess profits were considered immoral at one time. There was a time when a business considered 5 per cent or 6 per cent of profit on its sales was quite a good profit. Today we allow 300 per cent, 400 per cent 500 per cent profit. And if one cannot make that kind of profit, one is not considered a very good businessman. Therefore, there has been this disintegration of the moral structure to a great extent.
It is the responsibility of the major Governments of the country, the provincial and the federal Governments, to uphold the moral fibre of the country. What is being done in this Bill, and in any Bill of this kind, is the undermining of that structure. There is quite a difference between lotteries or "raffles",
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
as they are called, on a national basis and lotteries or raffles on a local basis. When someone comes to me in my own community to sell a ticket on a raffle, he does not spend a lot of time telling me what a great prize I am going to win if I buy this ticket. What he is actually asking me to do is to contribute very directly to something. I know that is implied in this Bill. However, if one looks at the advertising of lotteries across the country, one finds that it is not the basis on which that advertising is put forward. The advertising of both federal and provincial Governments has always been, "Spend a dollar and win a million. Be a millionaire all at once." The implication, therefore, of the Government's getting into this kind of "business", if you wish, is not in the best interest of the country.
As a number of other Hon. Members have already suggested this evening, besides the concern which we should all have as to whether this is good for the people of Canada, we have here a kind of typical Liberal approach to legislation as a whole. What the Government is suggesting here is that there are a number of items in the Bill which it knows we would like to support, things like the Olympics, culture, the development of the arts, medical research. These are things which it knows everyone is going to support. Therefore, it attaches them to a method of payment which many Hon. Members of this House, and many people across Canada-I would suggest possibly the majority-abhor. It is the method of paying for these benefits which they abhor, using the gambling instincts possibly, and appealing to greed to some extent. It is a method of supplying these benefits, which everyone wants, in such a way that it is difficult to take a stand against it.
However, it is important that we do put up a defence against this kind of development. The Government did the same thing last week with respect to the Crow Bill, which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) pushed through the House. Here again, there was something in this Bill which everyone supported, the development of the railways, the improvement of the railways. However, the method of payment was not supportable by a large portion of the population, at least those who were being asked to pay for it, the farmers of western Canada. Again, one sees the typical Liberal approach of putting in place something that is worthwhile and paying for it with something that is abhorrent.
The federal Government has a responsibility to control funding methods. There are other alternatives in funding these kinds of things. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) suggested direct taxation if we believe that these are the kinds of things we should be supporting and that they are good and necessary for the country. Then we should be quite willing to fund on a direct taxation basis. Also, there are parts of it that I am sure can be done on a straight contribution basis. Many parts of our sports and art structures are already funded on this basis. It can be continued or classified, allowing tax deductions if possible. The method being used and, again, I follow many other Hon. Members, is

June 27, 1983
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
indirect taxation, but it is one which is not in the least progressive. If one is making $1 million a year, a tax to buy one ticket will cost $10. If one is making $5,000 a year or barely surviving and one decides to buy the ticket, it will still cost $10. Therefore, it is a really regressive tax. If one has $1 million, why should one go out and spend $10 on a ten million to one chance of getting another $1 million? However, if one has only $5,000 a year, it seems like a pretty good idea to spend $10 in the hope that one can gain $1 million. Therefore, this regressive taxation becomes a very great factor. We should consequently remove that kind of method of funding.
Finally, this matter involves a Crown corporation. As the Hon. Member who last spoke said, the people of Canada have watched the Government's involvement with Crown corporations far so long that they no longer trust the ability of the Government to operate a Crown corporation well. This may be a valuable corporation, if it must be established. However, how can we be sure that the Government, which has done so badly in the past with Crown corporations, will operate this one any better than it did Canadair or any of the other large corporations which have lost accountability?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate this evening but I cannot say that I am happy to do so. Somehow I feel rather sad that this great institution that has such a tremendous responsibility and also an influence for good in our nation should have before it a Bill which I believe tends to erode the very ethical and moral basis and foundation of our country.
I cannot help but think back to when I wore a different hat, or collar. In preaching to my congregation, I would point out the fact that I believed that in the exchange of goods, there were only three principles that were operative: one was by purchase, the second was by barter and the third was an outright gift. When we move into the area in which we are moving with this particular Bill, we are bypassing those basic principles and carrying on one of the weaknesses of humanity, which seems to be becoming more prevalent in these days, that is, to try to get something for nothing, and get it quickly.
There are several components of the Bill that have been mentioned to which I want to refer very briefly again. First, I would start by referring to the matter which was addressed by the previous Hon. Member. His last comment concerned the fact that under the provisions of the Bill we are called upon to set up another Crown corporation. We must remember the words of the Auditor General when he referred to the Crown corporation proliferation as being a sub-government, one that was beyond the control of Parliament and one that did not have any sense of accountability.
When I think of another Crown corporation being set up at a time when there is so much criticism directed toward that type of activity, I somehow feel that we are moving in the wrong direction. We ought to call a halt and consider whether or not we are setting up just one more agency which will be
beyond the power of Parliament to control, one that does not have any sense of responsibility to the Canadian people.
Another matter in that connection is that we are called upon to amend the Criminal Code. Just to bring this to our attention, Clause 33 states:
The Criminal Code is amended by adding thereto, immediately after Section 188 thereof, the following Section:
"188.1 Notwithstanding any provision of this Part relating to gaming or
betting it is lawful
(a) for the Government of Canada to-
That is absolutely reprehensible. It is completely immoral to say that under the Criminal Code a thing is illegal and a crime, and then for the Government to bring in a measure and say, "We will put in a clause and say, regardless of what is in the Criminal Code, that we will do it and we will not be held responsible for it. We cannot be charged under the Criminal Code". What in the world is the Government thinking about? Where are we going in this country? It is absolutely wrong for a person or a community to do something, yet a Government can do it, wrapping itself in the garb of irresponsibility and saying, "In spite of what the Criminal Code says, we will do it and you cannot charge us for the crime". I wonder how much has been spent in pressuring people to do what is intrinsically wrong according to the Criminal Code. The Government will advertise and urge the people to do what is wrong according to the Criminal Code. I would like to know just how much money Governments have spent in the past in order to get people to do what I have suggested is wrong. May I say that the Government is completely irresponsible. It is immoral for a Government to do this.
It is asking us to go ahead and pass this measure. I believe that if the projects that are stated as being the recipients of assistance in this Bill are laudable causes, which they are, they should not be left to chance. They should be provided for from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and the money obtained in a legitimate fashion from the people of Canada instead of through the back door via this particular mechanism.
I know that the Government will say that we are advocating greater Government expenditures. But I can outline many projects which the Government could eliminate and transfer that money to meet the demands and requirements of these particular causes. I believe, along with other people in this country, that this is part of a larger plan to take much more power into the central jurisdiction of Canada. Howe could this be done with Canadians who have been raised on a broadly decentralized power in the country, with individual responsibility at the family and community level, a little less at the provincial level and a little less at the federal level? First, it would demoralize people in their own individual families and communities. One clear way to do that is to bankrupt them and make them even more dependent on a handout. Programs would then be introduced for people to receive a grant from the Government. They would soon learn to respond to that. They would be given the illusion of wealth by having them spend more money than is being taken from them. This is what we have seen since this Government came to power.
