The great problem, as I was explaining, is that the people who are systematically victimized are those who can least afford to be caught up in another process of wagering on the ultimate outcome of what will be a new gambling venture. It is important for us to recognize that in the event the Government of Canada has abandoned the usual raising of revenues, by any mode or system of taxation as it is authorized to do under the provisions of the Constitution, it should reflect upon using this particular mode of taxation which carries with it an induced voluntary element which I must confess will extract more revenues from Canadians. In this case very clearly the majority of revenues will come from people who are least able to pay them. From the standpoint of raising revenues, in the event that the Government approaches this matter in a businesslike fashion, ought it not to be concerned about the ultimate consequences of its other sources of guaranteed contract revenue from other lottery ventures in which it is indeed a partner?
The proliferation of lotteries with additional costs and expenses of advertising and promotion surely will not return, I suspect, the kind of revenues the Government of Canada expects to generate from its own individual effort, having regard to the funds that it has been assured of receiving from its joint businesslike partnership arrangement with the Provinces. To say that this venture, in competition with itself as a partner in another venture, is poor business is to put it as gently as I can. It is very clear, recognizing that there is a tendency among the people of Canada to wager on gaming or lottery type devices, that the Government wishes to have 100 per cent of the pie, in this case regardless of what those consequences may bring to it in terms of revenue generated otherwise.
Let me pass, if I may, to an issue that has been raised time and time again, that is, the great merits of the scheme, having regard to an obligation which the Government undertook with respect to the 1988 Calgary Olympics and the defence so often raised that this particular Bill is necessary in the event that money is in fact to be made available by the Government of Canada to fund a federal Government obligation to the Olympics. Very clearly the federal Government has that obligation. It has that obligation because these are national events in Canada conducted on an international scale. It is an obligation of the Government of Canada to support the worthwhile work of a city or community which has gone out on a limb and committed itself to bring to our country an event of the significance of the Olympic games in Calgary. The Government of Canada should be proud to participate and to carry
out its Ftndancial obligations rather than endeavour to push this Bill through the House, justifying its existence and coercing some to adhere to its passage on the basis that this is a panacea for the raising of funds for an international athletic meet.
If you examine the provisions of the Bill, you find that clearly that is but one of a variety of purposes allegedly advanced by the Government to induce Members of the House to support this piece of legislation. Under Clause 18(3) we find moneys may be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, to which moneys are ultimately paid by the corporation, on a fixed term out of the revenues of the corporation "for the support of one or more of the following activities". Then a group of activities is listed, one of which happens to be the 1988 Calgary Olympics.
In the event that this Bill was designed to accomplish the purpose alleged by the Government, I would have thought we would find a sunset clause built into the Bill which would have brought the existence of this corporation to a grinding halt when the required funding for the Olympics had come and gone, but that is not the case.
To pass on to another consideration, my great concern is the required financing. Here is a money-making operation that requires $10.5 million seed money to start. There are additional funds that may be advanced. They may be advanced by the Minister of Finance on the application of the corporation, approved by the Minister, and the total amount that may be advanced under those additional financing clauses by way of loan shall not exceed $20 million. Therefore, we are looking at $30.5 million. Having regard for the rather complicated fashion that has been gone through for the purpose of setting up this corporation, the corporation will probably go through that money in short order. We will have another drag on the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and the finances of this country through another Crown corporation would get out of hand as they habitually do, much to the detriment of the taxpayers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often that one gets such attention when rising to speak in the House when one has to interrupt the deliberations of the Chair. The importance of the Bill we are now considering warrants that kind of attention. We have heard many arguments raised against the provisions of this Bill. What we have
June 27, 1983

not delt with is the whole perception of this kind of legislation as it is introduced in the House of Commons. It is something we should spend some time considering.
It is a very simple matter to introduce in the House of Commons a Bill and make a claim amongst and to Members of the House of Commons and to the public as to what is the purpose and the purport of that kind of legislation. That is what we have in Bill C-95 which enacts the Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act. We are told that this Bill must have the approval of the House of Commons and must be passed in order to save the Olympics for Calgary. Surely it is a matter of perception that the purpose of this Bill is to deal with the Olympic games that are to be held in Calgary in 1984 and that the provisions of this Bill will save the Olympic games from financial ruin.
We on this side of the House know that that is not the real purpose of the Bill. If this were a Bill to aid and finance the Olympic games which are to take place in Calgary in the next year and bring credit to Canada, credit to the great Province of Alberta, credit to all athletes in Canada and across the world who participate in the Olympic games, we would of course favour it and devote our time and attention to its early passage. That is what the Government tries to sell us and the Canadian public as being the purpose of this Bill. It says, "Pass this Bill and the Olympics will be saved, not only for Calgary in 1988 but possibly for all time".
We want to stand here and tell the people of Canada through the medium of this debate on Bill C-95 that that is not the case. The case is that the Government wants to get back into the lottery business. It has seen this weakness on the part of the Canadian people. It has seen this desire on the part of the Canadian people, myself included, to get that pie in the sky, to get that million dollars from nowhere, to invest $10 and become a millionaire forever. It wants to play on that weakness of mine and of other Canadians.
The Government wants back in there because its sources of revenue have dried up. It can no longer tax Canadians in the ordinary way. It cannot impose another income tax, excise tax, sales tax and a tax on air transportation or ground transportation. We can go on and on with taxes. The Government has run out of taxes. Revenues are dried up, so it wants another tax, a voluntary tax. It has taxed the people of Canada to the limit and is now looking for other kinds of taxes. That is what Bill C-95 is all about. Don't kid yourself about that. Bill C-95 is another kind of tax. It is a voluntary tax. You do not have to pay this tax. If you are strong and you realize the percentage of winning is nearly nil and recognize that it is hard work that leads to success and not the luck of the draw, you will not be taxed. However, if you are looking for pie in the sky, for a better tomorrow, for $10 to win you a million dollars, here is the kind of tax you want to pay. That is what the Government is doing to the people of Canada.
The Government is sick of people putting up all this money in the form of a voluntary tax and its not getting any benefit, so it wants back into the field. The federal Government withdrew from the field under the Progressive Conservative Government. It considered this source of "taxation" one that
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
should behoove and apply to the Provinces of Canada rather than to federal authority which, in a traditional and practical way, has the real source of taxation, a tax on the income of the people.
You cannot go wrong with a tax on the income of people. It goes up and down with the economy. If you cannot get your money out of income tax, you are in big trouble. That is the kind of problem the Government of Canada has today. It is in big trouble because it cannot get all the money it needs to pay for all the services it provides from the basic income tax. It has to broaden its tax base. It has to go into areas occupied by the Provinces and municipalities to find those revenues. That is the reason for this insatiable appetite of the federal Government to collect money, not only by normal taxation but by the latest kind of taxation, that is, a lottery.
If you do not agree that this is a tax, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you about the pari-mutuel betting which has been in existence in Canada for over 50 years. That is a source of revenue to the Government of Canada and to the Provinces. It is betting and it is a tax. The Governments take 20 per cent of the revenue or, actually, up to 24 per cent. But that is done legitimately. The Government says to the people involved in pari-mutuel betting at race tracks, "Put all your money in a pool and we, the Government and the track that operates the pool and the races, will take a percentage." The Government gains the taxation resource from that activity in exactly that way. That is quite fair. Everybody knows the rules.
A lottery is no different in kind or in substance. It is the same. It is a betting or wagering activity. You put your money up, Mr. Speaker, and you take your chances. In this case, the difference is that the Government of Canada that is operating the sports pool endorsed by Bill C-95 will not tell you what your return is versus the taxation aspect, Mr. Speaker. That is the only difference between this Bill with its sports pool based on a lottery and pari-mutuel betting.
The Government will not tell you what its take is, Mr. Speaker. It will not tell you whether it is 20 per cent, which is a legitimate marginal take from a wagering activity, or whether it is more. The Government wants more. In fact, as I understand it, it wants 35 per cent. In normal wagering terms, that is unfair on the face of it. That is too much money to take from Canadian people who put their money in a pool that has one declared winner from amongst the people who have participated. One out of every three dollars is too much to take. It is not the traditional rule of 20 per cent applicable to pari-mutuel betting.
Even if Government Members are right, they are wrong. Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my voice to the discussion on the amendment that has been moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). It is important that we put what we are debating into perspective. I will repeat to some extent what I have said earlier, but I think it is well known in the House that I oppose gaming and lotteries and especially the way in which Governments, with their moral obligation to the citizens at large, use advertising which at best is questionable to entice people to get involved in lotteries. When Governments advertise that to purchase a lottery ticket is to buy a dream, the force of Government is behind that advertising to the degree that it is believed that if Government is doing it, it possibly should not or does not face the same kind of scrutiny as would be faced by a private individual who put forward a game of chance.
Second, the Government has indicated that it needs this lottery in order to fund the Calgary Olympics. It is surely known by anyone who has looked at the application made by the Calgary Olympic Committee that the only reason the International Olympic Committee recognized and gave approval to the bid from Calgary is that the Calgary sponsors had in their possession a letter stating that the Government of Canada (a), welcomed the Olympics to Canada and (b), would help with the financing of the Olympics. There was no question in the minds of the members of the International Olympic Committee that that support was conditional on whether Parliament would support a sports lottery or a stamp program or an official souvenir or artifact program in order to provide the federal portion of the funding necessary. The only criterion was that the letter was a valid letter from the Government of Canada, the invitation was valid and the financial support was guaranteed. That was it.
The amendment that has been proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines, brings directly into focus the deception that is being foisted on the House and the Canadian people by the Government through this Bill, because this Bill does not restrict itself only to the Calgary Olympics. The argument that the Government would like to see take root in Canadian society is that anyone who is against Bill C-95 is against the Olympics and against athletes competing one
against another. That is not the issue. The Government wants to get back into the gaming business and it is using the Calgary Olympics as the vehicle by which to do so. Let us be blunt about it. That is what it is.
I know that those of us who have been against Government involvement in the gaming business for some time have been described in various ways. We have been told that we cannot impose our code of morality on the general public. That, Mr. Speaker, is a specious argument at best. Surely every time legislation is passed, that legislation or the regulations flowing therefrom are meant to control or limit in some way the actions of members of society.
Another argument that is used is that gaming does not hurt and that it is voluntary. Gaming hurts, Mr. Speaker. It might not hurt the Members of the House who may put a few dollars into a pool at the time of the Stanley Cup playoffs or the Grey Cup game. All evidence shows that a disproportionate number of people who buy this type of lottery tickets are from the lower economic strata of society.
It is then argued that we cannot protect everyone from his or her own folly. The argument is that you cannot protect everyone from his or her folly. How much time is spent in this House debating social policy with the hope that the human condition will be improved? I think it is almost a violation of what the Government says it stands for to bring in this type of legislation.
The other argument that is put forward is that the Government would not otherwise be able to fund worthwhile projects but that now it can find the funding through lotteries or gaming. I have always held that if the project is valid, that is what the Canadian people should be told and the money should be raised in the same way that it is for everything else that is valid-through taxation.
There is another reason why the Government wants to be in the gaming business, Mr. Speaker. I have been harshly criticized for using this expression but I will use it again-lottery proceeds are a great slush fund for Governments. They can use the money, which they did not get through direct taxation, to hand out all kinds of largesse, a pier here and there, saying, "The Government is doing this for you". There has been too much of that in society already, Mr. Speaker. Surely when the federal Government is finally extricated from this mess it should not want to jump back in with both feet.
1 know it is not too common in the House any more to listen to what the churches have to say. But the churches are comprised of Canadians who have some very legitimate concerns about the direction that society takes and, 1 should like to think, they have a more perceptive view of what some of the steps taken today and some of the easy approvals that the House asks for such as in Bill C-95, can lead to.
I should like to put on record an except from a letter from the Lutheran Church in America-Canada Section, as follows:
June 27, 1983

At its March 10-12, 1983 meeting, the Executive Committee of the Lutheran Church in America-Canada Section adopted the following motion:
That the LCA-CS, on the basis of our position previously taken, go on
record as being opposed to Bill C-95 and that the Government be so informed.

This is the time to stop further Government promotion of gambling in Canada. The United Church of Canada concerned with the Government's refusal to understand its obligation to support morality in Canada rather than to undermine it. We hope that you will do whatever is in your power to stop Bill C-95 from becoming law in Canada. Refer you to the brief by the Interchurch Committee on Gambling and Lotteries circulated to the Communications and Culture Committee December 14, 1982, re C-95 which was sent to you at a later date.
I hope that the Government, including the public servants who are responsible for the Bill, will not sit back and look at the arguments advanced against Bill C-95 as coming from another age. What we are dealing with are some of the bedrocks on which society was formed-decency, morality and the Government upholding that morality. Bill C-95 does not do that, and 1 oppose it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in the debate on Bill C-95 with much the same feeling as that expressed by my colleagues who have already spoken. The Bill is supposed to be a refinement of benefits for the people of Canada, proposed by the Government, but I have not heard a Member of the Government try to make the case for the benefits that can be derived through lotteries.
In 1979 when the Conservative Government was in power, the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) was Minister in charge of the Fitness and Sports Directorate. In conjunction with the Provinces he and the Cabinet made the decision that if the Provinces wished to tax through lotteries they could do so, and that by giving up something that the federal Government had total control over, the federal Government would derive some benefit. To date the federal Government has derived almost $100 million but now it is trying again to involve itself in the lottery business, the gambling business, the gaming business.
1 come from a part of the country where the men and women on the farms are gambling every year-with mother nature and their expertise. I do not think they need a lottery to stimulate their blood; it is stimulated every year when it does not rain or when it hails or when mother nature causes problems.
What did the Government do with that $100 million? The B-ski team had to come home last year and some of the members were assessed for representing the country. The Government claimed that it did not have any money-but it had $100 million and it had the general revenue of the country with which to support those young men and women-those fine athletes who represent the country. Instead, it billed them additional charges and for travel.
In Clause 14 the Bill sets out the objects of the corporation as follows:
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
(1) The objects of the Corporation are (a) to organize, operate and manage, alone or jointly with the governments of any one or more provinces with which the Corporation has entered into an agreement or agreements for such purpose, pool systems in accordance with regulations made pursuant to section 16;
That is already in place, Mr. Speaker. The only difference is that the Provinces have control over it. The Provinces take the lead and if they feel that is the way they would like to assist and they would like to impose lotteries upon their people, then that is fine.
Why get the federal Government more deeply involved at this time in a process of taxation-for this is purely taxation and has nothing whatsoever to do with recreation or leisure? There is a hue and cry about the Calgary Olympics. I do not think any Member on either side of the House would deny the Calgary Olympics any funding that is necessary. I do not know anyone who wished to deny funding for the Montreal Olympics when they took place either. This Bill, Mr. Speaker, is not necessary in order to provide funding for the Calgary Olympics. I would like to see any one of the Hon. Members on the Government benches stand and explain why a lottery is necessary in order to provide funding for an Olympic-type games, a grandiose meeting of young men and women from across Canada and athletes from around the world. Why must we have a lottery to do that? More importantly, Mr. Speaker, the Calgary Olympics are about fourth on the list. Clause 18(3) of the Bill states, and I quote:
There shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to or for the support of any one or more of
(a)	activities in the following fields:
(i)	the arts and culture,

(iii)	medical and health research-
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), Mr. Speaker, stood in this House and condemned some of the methods used to provide health care by the Provinces because there is not enough funding provided by the federal Government and here we have a lottery put into place, Mr. Speaker-

I strongly support my colleagues who have spoken on it and appreciate the support which the churches have given to our Party in trying to stop this Bill. However, if one looks at the rationale, the reason behind people being put into the position of having to put out $5 or $10 every week or month to better themselves, it must fall on the shoulders of the Government; it must be a failure of the Government to provide another form, another way of getting ahead, another way of attaining that Canadian dream which so many people in this day and age under this administration have been denied. If the best that this Government can offer, Mr. Speaker, is a lottery, a chance of one in six million or one in ten million, I cannot help but know that it will suffer the eventual rejection by the people of Canada.
After the heading of the Winter Olympic Games to be held at Calgary, it is stated, and I quote:
(r) worthy capital projects of national interest in the fields described in subparagraphs (a)(i) and (ii)-
We do not even know, Mr. Speaker, what these "worthy capital projects" could be. The problem here is that the Government is asking us to pass a Bill with nothing definite in it. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) with respect to Bill C-95, an Act to provide for Government operated pool systems on combinations of athletic contests and events and to amend the Criminal Code and the Income Tax Act.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have before the House in Bill C-95 a Bill which legalizes in fact that which is now illegal. This is a Bill through which the Government imposes upon all Canadians, those who have a voice and those who do not, the legalization of gambling, lotteries, betting and pools. I would like to make very clear in this House, and to the people of Canada, that no one on this side of the House is against the Olympic Games being held in Calgary. We are not
against that noble, upright and honest purpose. We stand in support of our youth and of the people from various countries who compete. We stand behind them fully. I would suggest to this House, Mr. Speaker, and to the country of Canada, that the Canadian people would stand behind such a noble undertaking as the Olympic Games.
It was mentioned earlier by the Hon. Member for Kinders-ley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) that when the Olympic Games were held in Montreal, the Canadian people supported and backed them fully. The Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) read into the record the protests of two major denominations and many other churches which have sent protests to the various Hon. Members of this House against what is being done to encourage betting and gambling. The motive of the Olympics is a high one, but the direction in which the Government undertakes to finance it is absolutely demoralizing to the country and to its people. I suggest that I, for one, cannot support the direction being taken in Bill C-95.
You will notice it is the poor who will be hurt. It is the person who probably is not thinking at the time and who invests maybe his last $10 in something which he believes will make him a wealthy person. Therefore, it is a tax upon the poor.
What about the morality of this matter? I believe there must be a question of whether it is right for a Government to inflict this kind of legislation upon the people of this country in the way in which it is inflicted. It is bringing before this House legislation which, as I mentioned earlier, legalizes that which is illegal. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, to Hon. Members on the other side, particular by the Ministers, that if they would go to the Canadian people with a plebiscite on this type of legislation, asking them if they are willing to support athletic events in an upright and noble manner, the people of Canada would say, "Yes, we would." However, if the Government continues in the direction it has taken through the Bill, I would say that it would receive a big "no" from the people of Canada. People in general are not in favour of this type of legislation and this type of moral approach to athletics. The Government could find other ways.
If one considers the Crown corporation which is being put into place to create, to control and to conduct gambling, pooling and betting to support the athletic event in Calgary, one might ask oneself, in what other ways could a Government move? We should consider some of the outrageous spending of the Government and some of the Crown corporations, particularly Canadair, involving $1.4 billion.

describe how badly I feel that the Government has not lived up to the agreement.
Let me bring to the attention of the House the objectives and principles for the agreement we had with the provincial Government. With respect to arts and culture, the objectives were as follows: First, to assist activities within the arts, heritage and cultural industry sectors not otherwise possible on the basis of existing resources or programs; second, to promote public access to Canadian cultural works; third, to promote public participation in arts and heritage activities; and finally, to equalize opportunities to all Canadians to share in our cultural life.
Let me describe the principles for art and culture since the Minister wants to know. They are; First, to maximize opportunities for joint federal-provincial and, where possible, municipal or private sector participation in program or project funding; second, to avoid new funding programs which would require growth in federal government personnel; third, to design programs in a way that long-term financial dependence on this source of funding is not created, but that long-term benefits are realized in the arts, heritage or cultural industries sectors; fourth, to favour programs which benefit the general public over those which relate primarily to professional, organizational or other particular interests; fifth, to ensure that all dispensements of the funds are in accordance with standard government accountability practices; and sixth, to permit a greater federal share in joint programs or projects in those regions and communities which are economically disadvantaged.
Let me tell you what happened in fitness and amateur sport. Programs and projects must be designed to encourage, promote and develop fitness, amateur sport and physical recreation in Canada. The principles are as follows:
Programs/projects must be a national or international import, including research in the areas of fitness or amateur sport or physical recreation.
Programs/projects must be easily identifiable to the general public and thus be effectively promoted or advertised.
Programs/projects must be new in nature or be expansion of existing authorized ones.
Programs/projects which receive partial federal funding should be encouraged to obtain other necessary funding from other acceptable public and/or private sources.
Programs/projects which receive funding, must not be in conflict with provincial jurisdictional programs and/or projects of similar character.
Programs/projects requiring major capital costs will not be eligible.
Programs/projects which receive funding will be subject to T.B. directives re Grants and Contributions.

I bring this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because I heard the Minister say the only thing the Government had to give the Calgary Olympics, or part of the criteria when Government representatives went to Baden-Baden, was the stamp, coin and sports pool. There was no such thing as a sports pool. There was no such thing as saying to the people at Baden-Baden that there were coins and stamps. You do not do that before a professional body, the COA or the International Olympic Association. You say that you are going to be part and parcel of one-third, one-third and one-third; the municipality, the province and the federal Government.
Two applications were made. An application was made on behalf of Vancouver and an application on behalf of Calgary. Calgary was awarded the games. It did not matter who received it. The Government is committed to one-third of the capital costs of the projects. It is wrong for the Minister to deceive this House. I do not know whether he did that intentionally, but I find that these types of things do happen.
Let me talk about this agreement we made with the provinces, and I must say it was a very good agreement. Let me tell you what we did. Part of this agreement reads:
In view of the fact that this agreement is expected to result in increased earnings for provincial lotteries:
(a) the Provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec will assume responsibility for any Government of Canada share estimated to be $13.5 million of the costs relating to the expansion, upgrading and renovation of the NHL arenas in Edmonton, Winnipeg and Quebec City.

The Province of Alberta also looked after the Olds disaster fund in the amount of $2 million. The Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) helped negotiate that deal when we were in government. The Olds arena was burned down. We went ahead and had Alberta fund that $2 million.

Easy on the word "truth"? It is a word the Minister uses to describe himself and it is one that I would not use in a million years. When a Minister says that this piece of legislation must pass this House in order to provide funding for the Calgary Olympics it behooves every voter to read the Bill. If you read it carefully, Mr. Speaker, you will notice there is not a word guaranteeing that a penny raised will go to the Calgary Olympics. There is absolutely no requirement in this piece of legislation that a penny, a dime or a dollar, will go the Calgary Olympics. When a Minister goes to public meetings and to the media and says that we have to pass this Bill in order to provide money, you would think that an honest Minister would put into the piece of legislation the simple fact that if money is raised-and there seems to be some doubt whether money can be raised through this mechanism-it will go to the Calgary Olympics.
I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for St. Catharines. He has moved an amendment, the one we are debating now, that will guarantee that if money is raised it will go to the Calgary Olympics. If the Minister, the Cabinet, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal Party of Canada are telling Canadians the truth, that this piece of legislation is to provide money for the Calgary Olympics, then they should signal the fact in the House of Commons that they intend to vote for the amendment. They cannot have it both ways. They
cannot tell Canadians that they need it for funding and then refuse to include in the legislation that the funding will be used for the Calgary Olympics. If the Liberals rise in the House and vote against Motion No. 3, they will be clearly branded for the Canadian voters as liars. To vote against this amendment and to stand up and say the measure is necessary for the Olympics is to brand oneself in each and every individual case as a liar, because there is nothing in the legislation to indicate that one dime has to go to the Calgary Olympics.
The legislation indicates that the money, if it is raised, could be used for arts and culture, fitness and amateur sport and for medical and health research. The only item missing in that list of activities for an advertising manager who wants to promote the sale of lotteries is something to do with children. It is a peculiar list of human activities for which the profits of this fund are to be used. It is an advertisement agency dream, because who can be against arts and culture, fitness and amateur sport or, more important, medical and health research?
The Liberals are making a public statement about their personal morality and about their concept of Canadian society, that funding for these activities shall be chancy and depend upon the willingness of Canadians to bet. What a different statement we would have if the Liberal party of Canada said it wanted a sports lottery and the funding would go to drill oil wells, to put buoys in the ocean, to build a frigate or to build an atomic bomb. No, the Liberals say that those things will get their funding. Petro-Canada will get $400 million to drill oil wells but medical research will depend upon Canadians who want to bet and take a chance. In other words, they will fund medical research, arts and culture, and fitness and amateur sport from the back pockets of the poorest segment of Canadian society. Those things will be subject to the hazards of the willingness of Canadians to bet at any given point in time.
But they want to drill oil wells in the Arctic and to give the President of Petro-Canada his private jet to fly weekly back and forth to Calgary. They will ensure that that funding is secure; they put it in the budget and they have it for spending. But when it comes to an international commitment to amateur sport around the world, it will depend upon the willingness of the poorest segment of Canadian society to bet. If we want increased medical research, it will also depend upon the poorest segment of Canadian society.
The Government's morality and priorities are upside down. The reason for the list of activities in the Bill is to sell tickets, to encourage Canadians to bet. I would not be surprised after this speech to see a Liberal rise and suggest that some kind of charity for children be added to the list because that would help sell even more tickets. The purpose of the list is to sell tickets.
I would like to suggest one more test of the sincerity of the commitment of the Liberal Government. When this Bill is
June 27, 1983

pushed through the House, it will create jobs. There will be people needed to sell the lottery tickets. There are two million unemployed Canadians out there, some of whom are watching the House of Commons this evening. I suggest to every one of them that they write to the Prime Minister and say, "I want a job selling lottery tickets". They could go one step further. If they do not obtain the jobs, they could ask the Prime Minister for a list of those who got the jobs and ask him to put a little asterisk beside the ones who were on unemployment insurance or who were unemployed. 1 bet there will not be many asterisks, that those jobs will not go to unemployed Canadians. They could ask him to put two asterisks opposite the names of those who donated money to the Liberal Party in the last year, and I bet there would be quite a few of those asterisks.
We are not dealing tonight with a piece of legislation that makes any sense in relation to funding the Olympics. We have the experience of the Province of Quebec trying a similar idea which is going bankrupt. It will not make money, it will not get the job done. It leaves volunteers in the City of Calgary, people who are donating their time and effort to the success of this endeavour, on the horns of a dilemma. Because there is no guaranteed funding, they cannot plan.
The reputation of Canada is at stake in the international community. Our Party has made a firm commitment. If we were the government, and when we become the government we will write a cheque to the Calgary Olympic Authority and give it the money it needs to protect Canada's reputation in the international community. That is our promise, that is our commitment. It has been clear and it has been consistent.
I urge some free-thinking Members of the Liberal Party of Canada when the vote comes to be absent from the House or to have the courage to rise and vote against it. I encourage them to take their lead from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who stated in committee that she despised lotteries. We do not need one. We do not want one. We should keep our commitment to the Calgary Olympics, but we should get rid of this piece of legislation and move on to something else.

I want to read a press release which the Minister issued when he was discussing this Bill, to show the Canadian people how misleading he has been in presenting it. It is dated March 18, 1982. I quote:
By introducing the legislation now, Mr. Regan expressed the desire to see the Bill passed as expeditiously as possible, so that the new corporation can be established quickly and the sports pool game finalized and in operation. The Calgary Olympics will be given substantial financial support from Sports Pools revenues and it is important that funds become available soon so that the planning and preparation of facilities can begin.
That may not be the most misleading statement coming from that Minister, but it is one of the most misleading.
The planning and preparation of the facilities by the people in Calgary has been going on for a very long time. For the Minister to try and convince the people of Canada that the Olympics depends on the success of this sports pool or numbers racket is absolutely foolhardy. I can show that the moneys to
be received from this numbers racket, if it ever gets into place, will not be there for the Olympics. Let us look at where the money will go. The Minister is afraid to be specific. He thinks that Calgary will receive approximately 40 per cent of the net proceeds. He says that the net proceeds in one year will be about $100 million.
I want to go back to Loto Canada. In 1977-78 and 1978-79, the two full years it was in operation, lotteries were at their heyday. There was very little competition like there is today. In 1977-78, the net return to Loto Canada was $74,300,000. the following year 1978-79, it dropped dramatically to $62,471,000. At that time there was very little competition for lotteries, sports pools, or whatever you call them. It was going down rapidly when Loto Canada was put out of business, and rightly so.
Let us talk about the costs of those two years and the type of spending which the Government did on those lotteries. In 1977-78 they spent $10,400,000 on advertising and in 1978-79, $13 million. Ticket printing in 1977-78 was $3 million. It went to $8 million in 1978-79. Sales promotion went from $5 million to $7 million in one year. Public relations went from $322,000 in 1977-78 to $1,436,759 the following year. What did public relations take into account? I can see the staff giggling up there, but I want to tell Hon. Members that Loto Canada had a permanent hotel suite in the Four Seasons, outfitted with the finest of booze, food and entertainment all the time. The Chairman of Loto Canada had his own limousine and driver- nothing to it. That is where the money was being spent. That is why expenditures went from $322,000 to $1.4 million in one year.
Office supplies doubled in one year, $317,000 to $722,000. Furniture almost doubled from $250,000 to $402,000 in one year. Expenditures were phenomenal. This is why people do not want to see these great corporations, Crown corporations, established by this Government. They waste money, even though it is money raised by gambling, it is atrocious.
In our Motion No. 3 we say that we want the money to be slated for one purpose and one purpose only. If the Government is going to bring in this ill-conceived method of funding the Olympics as well as all the other things listed, then heaven knows where the money will go. We say it should be for the Olympics and the Olympics only. It should not be open-ended. There is no sunset clause and no real accounting to the Canadian people of what is going on. Some of the mess created in Loto Canada is now just coming to the fore, a mess created when it was being run by the Government that was then in power.
Let us take a hard look at Bill C-95, in particular where it says who will be the beneficiaries of this sports pool. It says there will be worthy capital projects in the area of fitness and amateur sports or arts and culture. Does that mean that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) will take money from this lottery to build a dome stadium in Toronto, for example? Is that what it says? It does not even define it clearly in the Act.

Member for St. Catharines put the amendment forward was specifically to try to hold the government to its word; that is, that the Bill restrict itself to the Calgary Olympics, despite the fact that this Party believes a commitment was made by the Government to the Canadian Olympic Association, and through that Association to the International Olympic Committee, and that those obligations should be honoured.

I am lukewarm at best to the amendment because of the promises made by the Government at the time of the Montreal Olympics. When I became a Member of this House, the first committee I was assigned to was Miscellaneous Estimates and the first Bill that committee was seized of was related to the sports loto, the stamp program and the coin program. 1 remember sitting on that committee, not until a quarter to ten or eleven o'clock, but until well past midnight. First of all the Government promised that the Olympics would be self-supporting. It said that these programs would take care of every obligation it had to the Montreal Olympics. Second, it said that the Olympics would be everyman's Olympics, they would be fun, they would be first class and they would be frugal.

That is why I say I do not believe this program will provide the funding. I will use the Calcuttas in Manitoba as an example and the numbers can be extrapolated for Canada.
The Calcuttas or betting pools on sports events were licensed by 77 organizations, according to an article in the Winnipeg Free Press on March 27, 1982. Keeping in mind that we are looking at a $100 million business in Manitoba, the profits as listed by the organizers of those 77 events totalled $26,000. If one starts looking at this numbers racket we are talking about today, and one starts taking a look at the money spent and the profits received, one can only feel the greatest sympathy for the organizers of the Olympics in Calgary. Those people deserve better, Mr. Speaker. They deserve that this Government keep its word.
My colleague from Edmonton, Mr. Speaker, mentioned that this Government had been involved in the earlier sports gaming business and had also supported professional sports. What thanks have the people of Saskatchewan, specifically the people of Saskatoon, received in the last months from the beneficiaries of this Government largesse? Several examples have been given today of instances where it has meant hardship and loss to families caught up on this kind of desire to gain instant wealth and prosperity. It has been pointed out, of course, that those who profit, do so at the expense of others.
I spent most of today travelling across Canada. Thursday night, while travelling home to beautiful British Columbia, I saw a most spectacular sight over the prairie Provinces, a sight which I have never seen before. We were flying just a few hundred feet above a cloud blanket which spread from horizon to horizon when an electrical storm developed. The clouds below were spectacularly lit up by discharges of electricity all across the sky. This went on for most of an hour. Those of us who had our eyes glued to the windows of the plane watching this spectacularly beautiful sight, little knew that below us that storm would bring tragedy and destruction to cities and people. It was only the next day that we read about some of those tragedies, about the lad in Edmonton who was swept away while in the street in front of his home and whose body has not yet been found; about the young woman who drowned in her car which was stalled in the middle of a street in Saskatoon. Therefore, what was so delightful and spectacularly beautiful to some of us who were above the storm evoked just the opposite reaction from those involved on the ground.
I suppose that is a simple demonstration of the principle that has been expounded over on this side of the House, that lotteries are beautiful to some and damaging to others. As such, I think they are incompatible with the spirit of Canada and should not be used by the Government of Canada as a form of taxation for any purpose, no matter how honourable or delightful the purpose.
We live in a unique country. We in Canada have a diversity that is part of our strength and our heritage and leads us to cherish our country beyond any other. There is a diversity in Canada in attitudes, the same as there is in typography. It is important that actions by the national Government of Canada do not abuse or offend large segments of society. This should be avoided if possible. I believe that a lottery for whatever purpose, under legislation provided by the Government of Canada, offends a great many Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I did speak on the measure once this evening, but we are now considering a further amendment and I have a few observations in connection with it. First, the Government's claim has been that the Bill must be passed in order to facilitate the holding of the Calgary games. The inference is that without the support of the Bill, the games are in jeopardy. However, I would submit that everyone knows that that is not true. The same serious argument was used by the Government in forcing the Crow Bill through the House. In its argumentation it stated that if the transportation system was to be upgraded, the statutory Crow rate had to go because, through the change that it was proposing, the money would be forthcoming to
assist the railway companies in upgrading and providing a better transportation system for Canada. I think everyone knows that that was not true. Everyone was in favour of the upgrading of our transportation system.
We think back to the days when a certain Minister of Transport said that the transportation system was a mess. The same could be said today because we remember the attempts of the railway companies to discourage passenger travel by making it almost impossible to make connections at various out of the way points and by using other techniques as well. We are still facing a situation in which the transportation system is inadequate to fulfill the purpose for which it was originally set in place. However, I would suggest that there are other options open to the transportation system than the method and the route that the Government was following in trying to destroy the statutory freight rates.
We are faced with the same situation again involving a very laudable project namely, the Calgary Olympics. I do not suppose anyone objects to the holding of the Calgary Olympics. I would say that it is a possibility that the greatest percentage of the people of Canada think it is a good idea, even though they may not be sports-minded. They say it is a good idea to encourage our athletes to participate in competition with those from other countries, and they would like to see it go ahead. However, now I say that the Government in implying that unless this particular measure goes through and the sports pool is set up, those games are in jeopardy. However, we all know, in and around this place, that if the Government wants to do something, it gets some money somewhere. If it wants to prop up an ailing industry, and many times some of its own followers can help it out in a tought spot, it can get the money all right. It can go and borrow and does not mind doing it at all. Yet if we are to have the Olympics, it says that we cannot do it that way. It says that we must put in a sports pool and get the money out of those people who are poor and hard up yet desperate to make a dollar in order to better their economic condition and so they will take a chance on buying tickets.
The Government is hypocritical in its attitude, in its proclamations, in its announcements, because it knows very well that there are other avenues that it can tap in order to ensure the holding of the Calgary Olympics. It can do so without forcing the Bill through the House as it is endeavouring to do at the present time.
There has been a question raised as to whether it is a lottery or a sports pool, or just what it is. However, we all know that it is just a gambling device. I would like to draw attention to the following statement. It was the concluding words of the joint Parliamentary Committee on Capital Punishment and Lotteries in the report which was made on July 31, 1956. It concluded with a very interesting statement:
That no useful purpose could be achieved by the institution of state lottery in Canada. It considered that the proper role of the state is to control and regulate such gambling activity as is permitted to private citizens by the general law, and
June 27, 1983

that it is not appropriate for the state to provide facilities for gambling to the public. The committee includes, in the prohibition of state lotteries in Canada, those which might be operated by provincial and municipal Governments as well as the federal Government.
We see that the joint committee that was studying this particular activity as well as others, came to the conclusion that this was no place for the federal Government to move in and establish a national gambling facility in order to try to finance operations.
This particular amendment with which we are dealing now concerns the activities in the following fields: the arts and culture, fitness and amateur sport, medical health and research, the Winter Olympic games to be held in Calgary, and worthy capital projects of national interest in fields described in other paragraphs.
As we look at this particular matter, the Government is arguing against itself when it says that the Olympics will not take place unless this is set up. However, it has listed the Olympics as number four in its priority projects that could expect funding from this particular facility.

The points have been made. This Bill makes gambling by the Government legal, yet if I were to go to someone's home to gamble, that would be illegal. The Criminal Code, to which we have all agreed, has said that gaming and betting houses are illegal and not an action which we should encourage in our society. This Bill says in blatant words that if the Government does this, it shall be legal. What kind of an Act is that? As my colleague says, we all know of people who have been charged for running gaming houses. They have gone to jail and paid the penalty, with the entire blight on their career that this has meant. Yet the Government said that it can run these same type of gaming houses and operations legally. That is not how our society works.

We have also heard great argument on the method of raising money. We have heard it said that what this Bill proposes is simply and intrinsically bad and immoral, let alone regressive and that it will impact upon the poor in the country far more than on those of us who are wealthy. This Bill is certainly morally debilitating.
We have heard the argument of Crown corporations. Do we really need another Crown corporation in this country with its president, vice-presidents and directors, all of whom will be paid enormous salaries and all of them appointed by that gang across there? The proof of the pudding is in the eating and Canadians have eaten some rather sour pudding, all at enormous cost.
The point is that we know that these Crown corporations never fail. It is a matter of statistics that if 100 private firms are established, at least 40 per cent or 50 per cent of them will fail just because of bad management or under-capitalization. Not one Crown corporation in 15 years has failed, with the result that we now have over 300 Crown corporations. When one looks at their subsidiary corporations and sub-subsidiaries, they become totally unaccountable to us, the people.
When these Crown corporations face difficulties, the taxpayers of the nation simply have to kick in more money, which means that there is less disposable income in the pockets of ordinary, honest hard-working Canadians. They are the Canadians who are getting black lung disease in our coals mines, the farmers who are losing arms and legs in machinery and others who pay the supreme price in order to survive and look after themselves. Yet the Government is taxing it away and other people are deciding how it will be spent.

It says that if people do the right thing and support the Liberal Party, show up in large numbers when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others travel through their towns, they will receive a grant. However, if the other group wants to stand on its own two feet independently, it will not get any Government largesse. That is wrong in principle. Nobody should have that kind of power over any other human being. Yet that is the kind of power that the Liberal Cabinet and Liberal backbenchers permit the Cabinet to have over and over again in our society.
Clause 18(3)(b) states that one of the recipients of the money will be:
-the XV Winter Olympic games to be held at Calgary, Alberta.

Every time the Government brings out a program there should be a corresponding tax so the citizens of the nation have a choice. We should have that one provision in our laws and governments that honour it.
If you remember, Mr. Speaker, in 1968 we had balanced budgets. We had a small national debt, yet we had a sound old age security system. We had guaranteed supplements, we had hospital insurance, we had post-secondary education and we had medicare. In 1968, we had all of the social programs and we still had balanced budgets. We had a small national debt. We had that because we had a productive society. Everybody was working and paying in a fair share of the taxes. The money was being redistributed. The only time we got into trouble was by following the Pied Piper. We were led down the garden path. The Government proposed programs and said, "Folks, you can keep your low capitalist tax because we are simply borrowing it." At first, only 5 per cent went to service the debt, then 15 per cent, then 20 per cent, then 25 per cent, and now over 30 per cent of every tax dollar has to service the debt. While the Government was getting us into the problem, we had enormously good programs, low capitalist tax, but the Government was borrowing the difference. Now the taxes are rising to meet the programs. People do not have the cash flow and they are dropping like flies. It is predictable. It is because they were led into a trap. We had the illusion of wealth when we did not have wealth at all. Now we are paying the penalty. Regretfully, because of the actions of that Government, because of those creeps opposite, our children and our grandchildren will have to accept a substantially reduced standard of living.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). If this Bill has any meaning at all, I am sure we will hear from the Minister who is now in the House and we will hear from other Members on the Government side as to their feelings on this amendment.
This amendment makes specific within this Bill something which the Minister, his Cabinet colleagues and Members on the Government side have been maintaining since the inception of this Bill. This Bill is specifically, without exception we hear, to promote the fifteenth Winter Olympics to be held in Calgary. We will be pleased to see the Minister and all his colleagues on the Government side voting to support this Bill because they have been telling the people of Calgary and the people of Canada that the only rationale for Bill C-95, the sport pools Bill, is for the Olympic games to be held in Calgary.
By definition the Winter Olympics to be held in Calgary in 1988 are a special event. We have never had Winter Olympics in Canada. If this is a special Bill for a special event, the Winter Olympics, then I can accept it. But we have culture and art in this country on a daily ongoing basis. We have fitness and amateur sport on a daily, yearly, ongoing basis. We have medical health and research on a daily, yearly, ongoing basis. Why are these specifics, medical health and research, fitness and amateur sport, arts and culture, not funded the way other programs are in our country? Why are they not funded with tax dollars? Why is the Government's revenue not used in an ordinary way for things that we have in our country on a daily basis? Why would the Government attach these things that are so important to the daily lives of Canadians to something that is special, a world class event such as the Calgary Olympics?
When the Minister made his proposal to the International Olympic Committee that Calgary would host, with the assistance of the federal Government, the fifteenth Olympiad, I am sure he did not have in place the legislation for a sports pool, 1 am sure he did not have in place the legislation for the stamps, and I am sure he did not have in place the legislation in place to stamp medals and medallions. What he did say was that the federal Government, in conjunction with the Province of Alberta and the municipality of the City of Calgary, would provide the funds necessary to sponsor and look after the fifteenth Olympiad. It is the same in any small part of Canada, in my riding of Kindersley-Lloydminster, that if a community wishes to go ahead with a project, it would be expected to provide some of the funding. The Province would expect to provide some of the funding. For projects of a larger size, the federal Government would be asked to become involved.
I have not seen any record in any debates in the House of Commons that there had to be a special lottery, a sports pool, made available so the citizens in other communities in Canada could benefit from a facility that would provide daily and
June 27, 1983

yearly recreation for them after the event had passed. I find it strange, Madam Speaker, that this Government would feel it necessary to fund the Calgary Olympics in a manner different from the way it treats projects in any other part of the country.
But when you look at this paragraph where the amendment applies, it reads:
There shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to or for the support of any one or more of
(a)	activities in the following fields:
(i)	the arts and culture,
(ii)	fitness and amateur sport, and
(iii)	medical and health research-
(b)	XV Winter Olympic games to be held at Calgary, Alberta, and
(c)	worthy capital projects of national interest in the fields described in subparagraphs (a)(i) and (ii)-
It does not say anything about medical and health research. Apparently now that is not in the national interest. I do not quite follow that. But the real kicker, and it is underlined in the Bill, is:
-the amounts paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund pursuant to this section.
It does not say anything about the amount. There is not one word about the amount of money to be available for the Calgary Olympics or any other portion of this Bill. It says that what is paid in shall be paid out. I am sure, Madam Speaker, that the Minister, when he rises in his place to tell us how he feels about this amendment, will support specifically the Calgary Olympics and he will tell us how much money is involved, because I do not see that in the Bill. My colleagues do not see it in the Bill. But we are being told of the whole life and death struggle of the fifteenth Olympics in Calgary and we do not know how much money is going to be made available. We do not know whether it will be all the money that is needed or whether it will be one-third of it. We do not know the proportion. Nor do we know from where the shortfall will come. If the shortfall is to come from taxation, I would suggest, so as to be fair and straightforward to the people of Canada, that the taxation be put in place now, that it be specific so the people organizing the games in Calgary will know how much funding they will receive from this Bill and will not be buying a pig in a poke.
In closing let me say that if a lottery is needed for medical research, for fitness and amateur sport, for culture and for the Olympics in this country, maybe the grain producers in western Canada would like to have a lottery so they would not have to pay additional costs for the transport of their grain under the Crow change coming forth from this Government. Maybe we should have a lottery so that Ottawa, the capital of Canada, can have a decent airport. Maybe we should have a lottery for any number of things. I find it strange, Madam Speaker, that in this Bill, excluding the Calgary Olympics which are a special event, the rest of the projects are daily programs, programs which the people of Canada would be only too pleased to pay for if they felt the funding and the taxation dollars were spent wisely, and that they would not object to it. I will be voting in favour of this amendment and I am sure

subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS- PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION. (B) FORM OF COMPENSATION
HUMAN RIGHTS-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS- PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION. (B) FORM OF COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the injustices done to Canadians of Japanese ancestry in Canada in 1942 in the evacuation, internment and confiscation of property, it need hardly be argued today, ought never to have happened. There was never any military reason for this kind of action and no pressure from the military authorities.
Adjournment Debate
Nor did the Civil Service ask for the evacuation. The Civil Service was certainly more knowledgeable than the politicians of the day. Nor did the RCMP who conducted investigations ask for it. No acts of sabotage were carried out, there was no espionage and no evidence that any was planned.
Japanese-Canadians even volunteered for military service and some actually served. Ken Adachi's book is truly titled "The Enemy That never Was". The pressure, unfortunately, was political. There was an appeal by unscrupulous politicians to racial hatred and fear on the part of white British Columbians. It is part of long-standing prejudices and was seen in the period before the war in the denial of full citizenship rights to orientals throughout the 1930s, especially the right to vote.
There never was any need for the evacuation and that it was motivated by prejudice can readily be seen in the treatment of Japanese Canadians after the war. For purposes of immigration Germans were put on the same basis as other Europeans in 1950, while in 1952 the Japanese were still treated as enemy aliens. The enfranchisement of Japanese Canadians occurred only in 1948. Wartime controls on Canadians of Japanese origin were kept on until 1949 so Canadians of Japanese origin were required to carry a permit from the RCMP to visit B.C. Some went to jail for not having a permit. Interned people were not allowed back to B.C. for years, and even later were not allowed to have their fishing permits back.
A scandal erupted on the issue of deportation of people who had requested repatriation to Japan. It was later found that the requests were often never understood. Some were coerced and wives and dependents were included in the deportation. Fortunately, deportation orders were eventually abandoned. As late as April 1947 a CCF motion in the House of Commons was defeated 105 to 31 to remove all restrictions on Japanese Canadians. Only four Liberals and two Conservatives voted with the CCF.
This might be the time to pay tribute to my predecessors in the CCF for their courageous work in fighting against prejudice and for fair treatment. There was Angus Maclnnis, J. S. Woodsworth and Andrew Brewin of Greenwood who was prominent in the compensation issue and the fight against deportation after the war.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) has made reference to the Royal Commission on Compensation for Japanese Canadians. I should like to note that the compensation provided was only partial. More than 22,000 people were uprooted and moved across Canada, yet there were only 1,434 claims. Estimates are that people received only one-third of the value of their loss. Claims were made for more than $7 million but only $2.5 million was paid. Some claimants received as little as $50. It was not possible for many people, upon their return, to take up the life they had left behind. They could not buy back their houses and boats or the property they had been forced to sell. The compensation did not take into account inflation, loss of wages, salaries or profits let alone the suffering and humiliation.

June 27, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The Royal Commission exonerated the custodians office which is to say that it did the job it was told to do. What a job that was. There has been no apology, no remorse, no recognition of the injustice which was done. I note also that the Canadian judicial system failed utterly to redress the wrongs.
In the United States, Japanese Americans were able to get some relief. It was inadequate, but there was some relief. In Canada, these people had no rights once the War Measures Act was declared. Legal action in Canada was confined to the period after the War Measures Act and, indeed, well after the War. Interestingly, it was the last appeal to the Privy Council in the United Kingdom on certain deportation orders which ended that history of appeal. I am sorry to say that the Privy Council failed rather miserably. It did not even allow the modest exception which our timid Supreme Court of Canada would have. This happened to be the first case which was decided in the new Supreme Court of Canada Buildings. It was certainly not a good beginning for that Court.
Since World War II, Japanese Canadians have become an integral part of Canadian society. Many have played a very special role as the conscience of Canada in the peace movement. We cannot forget, and, indeed, I believe it is relevant to the discussion before us now on the treatment of Japanese Canadians here in Canada that it was on Japan that the first two atomic bombs were exploded. I regret to say it was the same Mackenzie King who authorized the internment of Japanese Canadians in 1942, who also said it was fortunate that the bombs were used on the Japanese rather than on the white races of Europe.
Concrete proposals have been made for $50 million to be given to a foundation which would in turn make particular reparation and otherwise use the money for the promotion of racial harmony and human rights. Good projects have been proposed and this seems to be an eminently reasonable approach. Certainly, the Minister of Justice should continue consultations with appropriate organizations and individuals and come back to Parliament with a firm proposal. One requirement for the building of a better society is to admit frankly the mistakes of the past and seek to redress the harm done. Justice must be done to Canadians of Japanese ancestry and it is the responsibility of the Minister of Justice to take the next step.

subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE-CANADIANS- PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION. (B) FORM OF COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no question that one of the more striking episodes in our history is that of the treatment of Japanese-Canadians during the Second World War. During that war, Japanese-Canadians were detained in transfer centres and internment camps pursuant to regulations made under the War Measures Act, and their property was seized and their loyalty to Canada was questioned. In Canada, compensation for property losses suffered by about 1,300 persons was paid in 1950, in the amount of approximately $1.2 million, following an examination of the claims of Japanese-Canadians by a Commission headed by Mr. Justice Bird
between 1947 and 1950. The procedures for submitting claims were widely publicized at the time and the awards of compensation were made after careful examination of the legal and factual basis of each case.
As the Minister indicated in his answer before this House on June 9, 1983, this matter is indeed under consideration by the Government at this time. This is a complex matter. Claims other than those based on infringement of property rights would be particularly complicated, both factually and legally, and especially having regard to the considerable passage of time. The fact that the events took place so long ago makes it difficult to identify them, quantify them and redress them in a manner which balances all the legal and equitable interests at stake. There are no simple solutions to the claims of those interned during the war.
Japanese-Canadians will be holding a conference in the fall during which they will discuss their position with respect to these issues. The Government will be very interested in learning of the proposals presented at this conference, as the wish of Japanese-Canadians regarding the events of the war must necessarily be an important factor in determining what form of reparative action might be appropriate in the circumstances.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PERCENTAGE OF PROCUREMENT FROM MANITOBA SUPPLIERS. (B) REQUEST THAT MANITOBA ORDERS BE INCREASED
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PERCENTAGE OF PROCUREMENT FROM MANITOBA SUPPLIERS. (B) REQUEST THAT MANITOBA ORDERS BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on June 16, as recorded at page 26438 of Hansard, I asked a question of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) relative to the procurement policy of that Department. That Department had issued figures as to the amount of goods and services it had purchased from various Provinces of Canada.
For some period of time it has been the stated policy of the Government that the procurement of goods and services should be more equitably distributed across the country, a goal which the Government has stated and one which has been accepted by Members of the House. The Government stands condemned by its own figures. Its released figures would show that of contracts worth approximately $5 billion, the following purchase percentages apply: for Atlantic Canada, 7 per cent, for the two Provinces of Ontario and Quebec, 77 per cent and for the West, 15 per cent. Specifically for the Province of Manitoba, which was the focus of my question, the Government's own figures show that only 3.7 per cent of total procurement contracts by the Department of Supply and Services have been issued for suppliers and business people in the Province. The Government gives lip service to a procurement policy which is to be equitable and fairly distributed to all Provinces and to all regions, but its own figures would indicate that those are words only.
In defence, the Government states, "Those are past figures. The next figures will be better". How many times have we heard that the next figures will be better, that we are doing

June 27, 1983

better and that all we should do is to be patient? Manitobans, for too long, have been too patient with the Government.
It is surely incumbent on the Government to give clear indications of procurement policy whereby there will be a better, more fair and equitable distribution for moneys spent. It should be kept in mind that the moneys spent are taxpayers moneys. The Government has received those moneys, to be used wisely and properly, from all sectors of the country and from every citizen. Therefore, the Government should be very careful to encourage, through its purchasing program, fairness in distribution.
Another factor that must be kept in mind is that the Government will state that it does not have the distributors at certain points. Very often one of the reasons distributors are not available is because of the Government's procurement policy to begin with. Through centralisation, too often businesses which could have been established in other regions of the country have not received the same consideration as those in central Canada. It is hard for me to understand, as a person coming from the Prairies, that in Atlantic Canada where we have matters relating to the offshore, the coastline, search and rescue and the Armed Forces only 7 per cent of the total purchases of the Department of Supply and Services would come from that region.

I am saying that as one who does not come from that region. It just simply boggles my mind to think that there are no more than 7 per cent of entrepreneurs in Atlantic Canada who could have supplied those goods and services for the Government of Canada. Nor am I saying for a minute that the Government would go to those regions for purposes of regionalism only and that competitiveness should not apply. I have no doubt in my mind that those people, given an opportunity, would be as competitive as those in any other part of Canada. The same applies in the West.
The Minister of Supply and Services said that on the Prairies, specifically in Winnipeg, we have been involved in the aeronautical industry. 1 pointed out to him CAE. CAE has closed down. If that is an example of success, we can do without that success.
I am saying to the Parliamentary Secretary not to promise us better figures but to show us; show us by a very clear pattern how those figures will be changed in order that our business people in the regions will have the same consideration for competitive contracts as those in the two central Provinces. We are asking for tangible results, not promises or hope. Give us some tangible results. The Government has had enough time.
We hear much about regional disparity. We hear much about divisiveness in the country. Surely this would be one very straightforward means by which we could put action to the
Adjournment Debate
sentiments expressed by a Government that surely should have national policies in mind rather than regional considerations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Schroder (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-PERCENTAGE OF PROCUREMENT FROM MANITOBA SUPPLIERS. (B) REQUEST THAT MANITOBA ORDERS BE INCREASED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a plesure to rise in response to the Hon. Member's question on federal Government purchases in the Province of Manitoba. It is, of course, too early in the year to give an accurate estimate of purchases that will be made in this current fiscal year in Manitoba.
The figure of 3.7 per cent referred to by the questioner reflects the current figure of 1,247 contract documents issued in Manitoba for the first two months of this financial year by both our regional and headquarters offices, for a total dollar value of $13.3 million. Last year some 13,000 documents were issued for a total value of $151 million. On that scale these first few months auger well for the future of contracting in Manitoba. In fact, the amount of regional purchases in the Province of Manitoba has increased by 15 per cent per year over the past three fiscal years. In actual dollars, the total of contracts issued regionally in Manitoba has climbed from $34.2 million in 1980-81 to $47.3 million in 1982-83.
I am also pleased to say that there are contracts before Treasury Board at this moment that will be of significant benefit to Manitoba in the aerospace field. On this subject there will be further significant sums going to the Manitoba aerospace industry as part of the CF-18 offset program. The growth of our regional purchases in Manitoba is further confirmed by our recent opening of an extra sub-office in Shilo, reflecting DSS activity in Manitoba.
We are, as the Hon. Member may know, decentralized inasmuch as we operate a network of supply centres across the country. These centres are there to respond to the needs of the federal Government departments that are located in those regions. The number of contracts issued in any particular region depends, therefore, to a large degree on the program requirements of our customers in those areas.
In order to spread the economic advantages of federal procurement to as many of these regions as possible, we also arrange for regional purchasing of the majority of the goods and services that are requisitioned at headquarters here in Ottawa where this is practical in terms of achieving the best value for every dollar spent.
It follows therefore that in terms of percentages of contracts issued across the country, one must take into consideration the industrial base of the Provinces concerned. Obviously, a broad, highly industrialized economic base would naturally succeed in competing for and winning a higher percentage of contracts than one whose base is mainly agricultural. We can, after all, only expect contracts to be let to those companies that win them in open competition.
The Hon. Member must acknowledge that in this free enterprise country, open competition is the only way we can ensure fair and equal treatment to all potential suppliers. The fact that at any particular period one province may be more

June 27, 1983
Adjournment Debate
successful than another is based on its ability to compete at that time.
This nation has experienced the trauma of recession. It is now on the upturn and our collective economic future is brighter today than it has been for years. Simply witness the report of Statistics Canada that shows, our inflation rate to be 5.5 per cent, the lowest it has been in ten years. Over the past year, however, we have seen a cutback in Government spending resulting in a percentage drop in this spending to most Provinces across Canada.
